Under depth and trace ideal conditions, the ring is Gorenstein if and only if it is pseudo-Gorenstein. If the Cohen-Macaulay type is two, then the ring is level. For nearly Gorenstein and almost Gorenstein standard graded domains of dimension at least two, the ring is Gorenstein and level.
returned_results.name: Corollary ({\autoref{Thm:WOWOW} and \autoref{Thm:MainC}})

returned_results.slogan: For a numerical semigroup S with multiplicity e, if the associated graded ring G(S) is Cohen-Macaulay, then G(S) is Gorenstein exactly when S is symmetric and satisfies any one of several equivalent conditions. These conditions involve M-purity of S or the equality of certain Betti numbers at specific indices. The equivalences hold for some or all positive integers k. The statements are interchangeable and characterize the Gorenstein property under the given assumptions.
returned_results.name: Proposition 2.8

returned_results.slogan: A ring is Gorenstein if and only if it has a nonzero Cohen-Macaulay module with minimal multiplicity, finite Gorenstein dimension, and multiplicity at most twice the minimal number of generators. Equivalently, the ring has a Cohen-Macaulay module with minimal multiplicity, multiplicity strictly less than twice the minimal number of generators, and vanishing Ext modules in high degrees. Another equivalent condition is the existence of two nonzero Cohen-Macaulay modules, one with multiplicity strictly less than twice its minimal number of generators and vanishing Ext in high degrees with the other, and the other having finite projective dimension. These conditions characterize Gorenstein rings.
returned_results.name: Corollary 5.1

returned_results.slogan: The associated graded ring of R with respect to the maximal ideal is Gorenstein if and only if it is Cohen-Macaulay and the set of maximal elements in the Apéry set with respect to a monomial order has exactly one element.
returned_results.name: Proposition 4.11

returned_results.slogan: A two-dimensional Cohen-Macaulay local ring that is locally Gorenstein on its punctured spectrum is Gorenstein if and only if any one of several conditions holds. These conditions include the vanishing of a specific Ext module, finite projective dimension of the dual of the canonical module, or finite complete intersection dimension and projective dimension of a certain dual module. The equivalence links Gorensteinness to homological and module-theoretic properties.

trajectory.query: stable weak solution approximation by smooth stable solutions semilinear elliptic equation mollification local Dirichlet problem stability preserved

returned_results.slogan: For dimensions at least two, every locally stable weak solution to a certain equation can be approximated by smooth stable solutions on a small ball around any point. The approximating solutions solve a regularized version of the original equation. The convergence to the original solution occurs in the Sobolev space norm. The radius of the ball and the regularization parameter depend on the point, dimension, and nonlinearity.
returned_results.name: Theorem 1.3

returned_results.slogan: A stable weak solution to the equation in the unit ball is either twice continuously differentiable, with the nonlinearity being Lipschitz on the relevant range, or it can be approximated by a sequence of smooth stable solutions. These approximations use nonlinearities that are bounded above by the original and converge to it pointwise. The approximating solutions are also bounded above by the original solution and converge to it almost everywhere and weakly. Each approximating nonlinearity is Lipschitz on the range of its corresponding solution.
returned_results.name: Proposition 18

returned_results.slogan: Given a bounded domain and a nonnegative stable solution to an equation involving a convex nondecreasing function, there exists a sequence of smooth approximations. These approximations are stable weak solutions to a perturbed equation and converge to the original solution in both the H1 norm and almost everywhere. Under additional boundary regularity and zero trace assumptions, the approximations exhibit higher regularity near the boundary portion. If the original solution has zero boundary values, the approximations can also be chosen with compact support and further boundary regularity.
returned_results.name: Proposition 21

returned_results.slogan: The theorem states that for a weak solution to a stochastic differential equation with a given initial condition, the expected supremum of the squared difference between the integral of a function and its mollified approximation converges to zero as the approximation parameter increases. This holds for any function in a specified class. The mollified function is defined by convolution with a smoothing kernel. The result applies over any finite time interval.
returned_results.name: Lemma 5.1

returned_results.slogan: The solution to the mollified stochastic differential equation converges weakly to the solution of the original equation.
returned_results.name: Theorem 5.1

returned_results.slogan: A stable weak solution to a fractional semilinear equation with a strictly convex nonlinearity can be approximated by a sequence of bounded stable solutions. These approximate solutions correspond to a sequence of globally Lipschitz convex nonlinearities converging to the original function. The approximations are bounded below by a constant and above by the original solution, and they converge to it in a Sobolev space. If the original nonlinearity is nonnegative or Holder continuous, the approximating sequence inherits these properties.
returned_results.name: Theorem 1.9

returned_results.slogan: A locally integrable function with compact support and a weak derivative has a smooth mollification. The derivative of the mollification equals the convolution of the mollifier with the weak derivative. The derivatives of the mollification converge to the weak derivative in local L1 norm. They also converge pointwise almost everywhere on the set where the weak derivative is locally integrable.
returned_results.name: Theorem 2.3

returned_results.slogan: A weak solution in a given domain can be approximated by a sequence of smooth solutions to a regularized problem. These smooth solutions converge to the weak solution uniformly on compact subsets and weakly in the Sobolev norm. The approximation occurs within any smaller subdomain compactly contained in the original domain. The regularized problem's structure conditions depend only on the original parameters.
returned_results.name: Corollary 2.3

returned_results.slogan: A strong solution u is convolved with a sequence of smooth mollifiers. The convolution yields a strong solution of the same equation. This convolved solution converges uniformly to u on compact subsets. The convergence holds over the time interval from zero to T and across the spatial domain.
returned_results.name: Lemma 3.2

returned_results.slogan: For a bounded smooth domain and a nondecreasing convex function with positive value at zero, every stable weak solution of the semilinear problem yields a family of stable solutions for a perturbed equation. Each perturbed solution corresponds to a parameter between zero and one and satisfies a fractional Laplacian equation with scaled right-hand side. These solutions are bounded and vanish outside the domain. Consequently, each is a classical pointwise solution.
returned_results.name: Lemma 4.4

trajectory.query: approximate W1,2_loc stable solution by C2 stable solutions -Delta u = f(u) local approximation

returned_results.slogan: For dimensions at least two, every locally stable weak solution to a certain equation can be approximated by smooth stable solutions on a small ball around any point. The approximating solutions solve a regularized version of the original equation. The convergence to the original solution occurs in the Sobolev space norm. The radius of the ball and the regularization parameter depend on the point, dimension, and nonlinearity.
returned_results.name: Theorem 1.3

returned_results.slogan: A stable weak solution to the equation in the unit ball is either twice continuously differentiable, with the nonlinearity being Lipschitz on the relevant range, or it can be approximated by a sequence of smooth stable solutions. These approximations use nonlinearities that are bounded above by the original and converge to it pointwise. The approximating solutions are also bounded above by the original solution and converge to it almost everywhere and weakly. Each approximating nonlinearity is Lipschitz on the range of its corresponding solution.
returned_results.name: Proposition 18

returned_results.slogan: Given a normalized viscosity solution u and a function f with bounded and continuous properties, for any positive delta there exists a small epsilon. If the norm of f and the deviation of p from 2 are less than epsilon, then there is a twice continuously differentiable function h. The difference between u and h is less than delta uniformly on a smaller domain. This approximation holds under the given smallness conditions.
returned_results.name: Lemma 3.1 (Approximation Lemma)

returned_results.slogan: Given a convex function f and a stable solution u to a semilinear equation, there exist sequences of convex functions f_k and functions u_k that approximate f and u. The functions u_k are stable weak solutions to equations involving f_k, with u_k converging to u in H1 and almost everywhere. Each u_k is bounded between 0 and u and agrees with u on the boundary. If f is nonnegative, then each approximating function f_k is also nonnegative.
returned_results.name: Theorem 5

returned_results.slogan: Given a bounded domain and a nonnegative stable solution to an equation involving a convex nondecreasing function, there exists a sequence of smooth approximations. These approximations are stable weak solutions to a perturbed equation and converge to the original solution in both the H1 norm and almost everywhere. Under additional boundary regularity and zero trace assumptions, the approximations exhibit higher regularity near the boundary portion. If the original solution has zero boundary values, the approximations can also be chosen with compact support and further boundary regularity.
returned_results.name: Proposition 21

returned_results.slogan: Assume A is a bounded and continuously differentiable function satisfying a given condition, and f is square integrable. Then the unique weak solution u_0 belongs to a local Sobolev space of second order derivatives in L2. The sequence of approximate solutions u_epsilon converges to u_0 in that same local Sobolev space. Additionally, certain scaled second derivatives of u_epsilon converge to zero in the local L2 sense.
returned_results.name: Theorem 1

returned_results.slogan: Given a bounded weak solution in a Sobolev space, if the exponent p is close to 2 and the function f has small L-infinity norm, then there exists a C1 function with small magnitude and small derivative such that the sum of the solution and this function is harmonic in most of the domain.
returned_results.name: Proposition 2 (Existence of small correctors)

returned_results.slogan: Under certain assumptions, a function w with local Sobolev regularity and finite norm for H(x, Dw) in L^(1+delta') over bounded subsets admits a sequence of smooth local approximations. These approximations converge to w in the Sobolev space W^(1, p(1+delta')) on any bounded open set. The L^1 norm of H(x, D tilde w_j) converges to that of H(x, Dw). Similarly, the L^(1+delta') norm of H(x, D tilde w_j) converges to that of H(x, w).
returned_results.name: Lemma 3.1

returned_results.slogan: A sequence of solutions converges weakly in L2 to a limit function. Under the assumptions of Theorem 2, this limit function belongs to the local Sobolev space H1.
returned_results.name: Corollary 3

returned_results.slogan: A continuous function solving an equation in viscosity sense can be approximated by a function solving a simpler equation. The approximating function has bounded second-order derivatives in a Sobolev space. The approximation is close in uniform norm on a smaller ball. The constants depend only on universal parameters.
returned_results.name: Proposition 3.3 (Second Approximation Lemma)

trajectory.query: stability inequality preserved under approximation semilinear elliptic equation smooth nonlinearities

returned_results.slogan: A stable weak solution to a fractional semilinear equation with a strictly convex nonlinearity can be approximated by a sequence of bounded stable solutions. These approximate solutions correspond to a sequence of globally Lipschitz convex nonlinearities converging to the original function. The approximations are bounded below by a constant and above by the original solution, and they converge to it in a Sobolev space. If the original nonlinearity is nonnegative or Holder continuous, the approximating sequence inherits these properties.
returned_results.name: Theorem 1.9

returned_results.slogan: A stable weak solution to the equation in the unit ball is either twice continuously differentiable, with the nonlinearity being Lipschitz on the relevant range, or it can be approximated by a sequence of smooth stable solutions. These approximations use nonlinearities that are bounded above by the original and converge to it pointwise. The approximating solutions are also bounded above by the original solution and converge to it almost everywhere and weakly. Each approximating nonlinearity is Lipschitz on the range of its corresponding solution.
returned_results.name: Proposition 18

returned_results.slogan: Given a convex function f and a stable solution u to a semilinear equation, there exist sequences of convex functions f_k and functions u_k that approximate f and u. The functions u_k are stable weak solutions to equations involving f_k, with u_k converging to u in H1 and almost everywhere. Each u_k is bounded between 0 and u and agrees with u on the boundary. If f is nonnegative, then each approximating function f_k is also nonnegative.
returned_results.name: Theorem 5

returned_results.slogan: For dimensions at least two, every locally stable weak solution to a certain equation can be approximated by smooth stable solutions on a small ball around any point. The approximating solutions solve a regularized version of the original equation. The convergence to the original solution occurs in the Sobolev space norm. The radius of the ball and the regularization parameter depend on the point, dimension, and nonlinearity.
returned_results.name: Theorem 1.3

returned_results.slogan: Given a bounded domain and a nonnegative stable solution to an equation involving a convex nondecreasing function, there exists a sequence of smooth approximations. These approximations are stable weak solutions to a perturbed equation and converge to the original solution in both the H1 norm and almost everywhere. Under additional boundary regularity and zero trace assumptions, the approximations exhibit higher regularity near the boundary portion. If the original solution has zero boundary values, the approximations can also be chosen with compact support and further boundary regularity.
returned_results.name: Proposition 21

returned_results.slogan: Given upper-semicontinuous functions with values bounded away from zero, an inequality involving their transformed sums holds. For any positive s, there exist uniformly continuous approximations of these functions that also satisfy the same inequality. These approximations converge pointwise to the original functions as s approaches zero. The result provides a smoothing technique while preserving the functional inequality.
returned_results.name: Lemma 4.7

returned_results.slogan: A unique viscosity solution u of a PDE converges locally uniformly to a stable solution u-epsilon of a consistent, nearly elliptic approximation scheme as epsilon approaches zero. This convergence holds when the non-monotone perturbation is continuous. Under these conditions, u-epsilon exists and remains stable.
returned_results.name: Theorem 3.5 (Convergence of Nearly Monotone Schemes~ \cite{ObermanFroeseFiltered})

returned_results.slogan: A continuous viscosity subsolution of a certain partial differential inequality can be approximated by sequences of smooth functions. These sequences converge uniformly to the original subsolution and a given function on a slightly smaller domain. The smooth approximations satisfy a modified inequality involving a divergence term. The modification includes an error term that depends on the regularity of a coefficient matrix.
returned_results.name: Lemma 5.3

returned_results.slogan: A locally integrable function satisfying a weak differential inequality has a sequence of smooth approximations. These approximations also satisfy the differential inequality and form a nonincreasing sequence. The sequence converges to the original function in an L1 sense on a smaller domain. The pointwise limit is upper semicontinuous and equals the original function almost everywhere.
returned_results.name: Theorem 9.1 (Littman)

returned_results.slogan: A continuous viscosity solution to an elliptic equation can be approximated by a sequence of functions with better regularity. These approximating functions belong to a local Sobolev space and satisfy a perturbed elliptic condition. The sequence converges uniformly on compact subsets to the original solution. This holds for any positive perturbation parameter.
returned_results.name: Theorem 9.1

trajectory.query: weak derivative of mollification equals mollification of weak derivative convergence in W1,2 local Friedrichs mollifier

returned_results.slogan: A locally integrable function with compact support and a weak derivative has a smooth mollification. The derivative of the mollification equals the convolution of the mollifier with the weak derivative. The derivatives of the mollification converge to the weak derivative in local L1 norm. They also converge pointwise almost everywhere on the set where the weak derivative is locally integrable.
returned_results.name: Theorem 2.3

returned_results.slogan: The convolution of a function with a mollifier commutes with multiplication by a function under certain conditions. If the function has a bounded weak derivative and the other function is locally square integrable, then the commutator of the product and the partial derivative converges to zero. This convergence occurs in the L2 norm on every compact subset as the mollification parameter approaches zero. The result holds for each partial derivative in the space.
returned_results.name: Lemma D.1

returned_results.slogan: For a function w in a Sobolev space with finite p, the mollification of its weak derivative of order alpha equals the weak derivative of the mollification of w. This holds for all multi-indices alpha with order at most k.
returned_results.name: Lemma A.6

returned_results.slogan: The derivative of the convolution of a function f with a mollifier equals the convolution of the derivative of f with the same mollifier. This holds for functions f in the Sobolev space W^{1,2} over the real line with values in a Hilbert space H. The result is valid for any positive parameter mu.
returned_results.name: Lemma A.26

returned_results.slogan: If a function's left or right fractional derivative exists locally in L1, then the mollified function's fractional derivative equals the convolution of the mollifier with the original fractional derivative almost everywhere.
returned_results.name: Lemma

returned_results.slogan: If a function's fractional derivative exists locally in L1, then the mollified function's fractional derivative equals the convolution of the mollifier with the original fractional derivative almost everywhere in a restricted domain. This holds using the standard mollifier and the mollification of the function.
returned_results.name: Lemma

returned_results.slogan: The fractional divergence of the convolution of a mollifier with a compactly supported Lipschitz vector field equals the convolution of the mollifier with the fractional divergence of the field. For a function of bounded fractional variation, the fractional derivative of its mollification equals the convolution of the mollifier with the fractional derivative measure. This fractional derivative measure of the mollified function converges weakly to the original fractional derivative measure as the mollification parameter approaches zero.
returned_results.name: Lemma 3.5 (Convolution with standard mollifiers)

returned_results.slogan: A function F with locally integrable weak derivatives has its singular set contained in the union of the singular sets of its derivatives. For a mollifier, the mollified F converges pointwise to F outside the singular set of F. Similarly, the mollified derivatives converge pointwise to the derivatives outside their own singular sets. The derivative of the mollified F also converges to the derivative.
returned_results.name: Lemma B.4

returned_results.slogan: The convolution of a locally integrable function with a mollifier yields a smooth function on a slightly smaller domain. This smooth approximation converges to the original function almost everywhere as the mollifier parameter approaches zero. For continuous functions, the convergence is uniform on compact subsets, and for locally q-integrable functions, convergence occurs in the local Lq norm. If the function is weakly differentiable with a locally integrable derivative, the derivative of the mollified function equals the convolution of the mollifier with the weak derivative.
returned_results.name: Lemma A.5 (Properties of mollifiers)

returned_results.slogan: The divergence of a smoothed version of a function converges weakly to the divergence of the original function in the L2 space. This holds for functions that are square integrable over the domain. The smoothing is done using a standard mollifier. The convergence is in the weak topology of L2.
returned_results.name: Lemma 13

trajectory.query: solve local Dirichlet problem for -Delta v = g with smooth g and boundary data existence uniqueness C2 ball semilinear elliptic

returned_results.slogan: Under an exterior sphere condition and strict ellipticity, the Dirichlet problem has a unique classical solution with interior and boundary regularity. If the boundary and data are sufficiently smooth, the solution is globally smooth with a Holder continuous second derivative. The solution's norm is bounded by a constant times the norms of the source and boundary data. The constant does not depend on the solution or the input functions.
returned_results.name: Theorem 2.24 (existence)

returned_results.slogan: Under certain conditions, a unique Lipschitz classical solution exists for the Dirichlet problem on a ball. The equation involves a second-order elliptic operator with a nonlinear gradient term. The solution matches given boundary data. If the coefficients are sufficiently smooth, the solution has higher regularity inside the ball.
returned_results.name: Lemma 6.2 (Semi-linear Dirichlet problem)

returned_results.slogan: For every positive continuous function on the boundary of a ball, the semilinear Dirichlet problem with a given nonlinearity has a unique positive continuous solution on the closed ball.
returned_results.name: Theorem 6.3

returned_results.slogan: A unique solution exists for the Dirichlet problem on a ball. The solution is continuous on the closed ball and twice continuously differentiable with Hölder continuous second derivatives on the ball union an open subset of the boundary. The boundary data is continuous on the entire boundary and has higher regularity on that open subset.
returned_results.name: Theorem 2.15 (Solution on a smooth boundary portion for Balls)

returned_results.slogan: For a ball of radius R, given boundary data g and a function f with certain smoothness, the Dirichlet problem for the operator L has a unique solution. The solution possesses second derivatives that are Hölder continuous up to the boundary.
returned_results.name: Theorem 2.14 (Solution on ball)

returned_results.slogan: Given a function w with bounded C two alpha norm on the unit ball, there exists a unique solution rho in C two alpha on the closed ball to a Dirichlet problem involving an operator L sub G of w and a given function g. The solution satisfies a boundary condition of zero on the sphere. The norm of rho in C two alpha is bounded by a constant times the norm of g in C alpha. The constant depends on parameters A, tau, and the C two one norm of f, and is independent of epsilon for sufficiently small epsilon.
returned_results.name: Lemma 3.3

returned_results.slogan: Given a closed ball in n-dimensional space, consider a twice continuously differentiable function F satisfying certain conditions. For any sufficiently smooth boundary data f, the unique solution u to the specified semilinear elliptic equation with Dirichlet boundary conditions exists. The absolute value of u at the center of the ball is bounded by a constant C. This constant does not depend on the choice of boundary function f.
returned_results.name: Lemma 3.1

returned_results.slogan: A domain with an exterior sphere condition on its boundary guarantees a unique solution to a specific Dirichlet problem. The solution is continuous on the closed domain and twice continuously differentiable inside. The equation involves the Laplacian of the function equaling a nonlinear expression involving its gradient and a given function H. The boundary condition matches a prescribed continuous function g.
returned_results.name: Proposition 4.11

returned_results.slogan: For a fixed point and positive constant, there exists a small radius depending on curvature, the constant, and dimension. Within balls of this radius, a specific Dirichlet problem involving a divergence equation is considered. The problem has a unique solution that is twice continuously differentiable inside the ball and continuous on its closure. This holds for any continuous boundary data on the sphere.
returned_results.name: Theorem B.9

returned_results.slogan: A continuously differentiable function g is given on the closure of a ball. A bilinear form is bounded and coercive on the Sobolev space of functions with zero boundary values. Under these conditions, a weak solution exists in the Sobolev space for a second-order elliptic partial differential equation. The solution satisfies a Dirichlet boundary condition equal to g.
returned_results.name: Lemma 3

trajectory.query: binomial edge ideal cut set minimal prime height dimension components D_S v-number local v-number colon ideal P_S

returned_results.slogan: For a graph G on n vertices, the prime ideal P_S(G) has height n minus the number of components plus the size of S. The binomial edge ideal J_G equals the intersection of all P_S(G) over subsets S of the vertices. If G is connected, then P_S(G) is a minimal prime of J_G exactly when S is empty or when removing any element from S increases the number of connected components.
returned_results.name: Theorem 3.1 ({\cite{HHHKR}})

returned_results.slogan: For a connected simple graph on n vertices, a prime ideal is defined for each subset S of vertices. The height of this ideal is given by twice the size of S plus n minus the number of connected components after removing S. The binomial edge ideal equals the intersection of these prime ideals over all subsets S. The prime ideal is a minimal prime if S is empty or if removing any single vertex from S decreases the number of connected components.
returned_results.name: Proposition 3.2 ({\cite[Lemma 3.1, Theorem 3.2, Corollary 3.9]{herzog2010binomial}})

returned_results.slogan: For a Cohen-Macaulay closed graph, the v-number of the binomial edge ideal corresponding to any cut set S equals twice the size of S plus the number of dominating vertices in S.
returned_results.name: Theorem 3.4

returned_results.slogan: For any vertex v in a simple graph G, the v-number of the graph's binomial edge ideal is at most one more than that of the graph with v removed. If there is a cutset T not containing v such that the v-number equals the T-v-number, then the v-number of the graph with v removed is at most that of G. If there is a cutset T containing v with the same equality, then the v-number of the graph with v deleted is at most that of G.
returned_results.name: Proposition 3.3

returned_results.slogan: The binomial edge ideal of a graph has a height equal to the number of vertices minus the number of connected components.
returned_results.name: Lemma 3.4

returned_results.slogan: A connected simple graph G has a vertex set from 1 to d. A subset S of these vertices defines a prime ideal related to the graph's binomial edge ideal. The prime is minimal if S is empty. Alternatively, the prime is minimal if removing any single vertex from S strictly reduces the number of connected components in the induced subgraph.
returned_results.name: Proposition 2.7 ({\cite{MR2669070}})

returned_results.slogan: For a connected graph G on n vertices with a minimal cut S, the v-number of the prime ideal associated to S equals the connected domination number of the bipartition defined by S. This number is the minimum size of a set A contained in the union of the two parts of the bipartition. The set A must have the property that its intersection with each part is a connected dominating set in the subgraph induced by that part along with the cut. This characterizes the v-number in terms of connected domination across the bipartition.
returned_results.name: Theorem 4.17

returned_results.slogan: The binomial edge ideal of a graph equals the intersection of prime ideals associated to its cut sets. Each prime ideal corresponds to a set of vertices whose removal increases the number of connected components. This intersection provides the primary decomposition of the ideal. The result holds for any graph.
returned_results.name: Theorem

returned_results.slogan: For a simple graph G, if A is in the set A_G, then the colon ideal of the edge ideal I(G) with respect to the monomial x_A equals the ideal generated by the neighbors of A. If the colon ideal of I(G) with respect to some polynomial f is a prime ideal in the set of associated primes, then there exists a set A in A_G with size at most the degree of f such that the colon ideal with respect to x_A equals that prime ideal. The v-number of I(G) is the minimum size of any set A in A_G.
returned_results.name: Lemma 2.5

returned_results.slogan: For a graph G on n vertices, a set T of vertices defines a prime ideal P_T(G) associated with the graph's binomial edge ideal. The height of this ideal equals n minus the number of components in G without T, plus the size of T. Every minimal prime ideal of the binomial edge ideal arises in this way from some subset T. The subset T must be empty or satisfy that removing any element from T reduces the number of connected components.
returned_results.name: Proposition 2.4 ({\cite[Lemma 3.1, Corollary 3.9]{herzog2010binomial}})

trajectory.query: Cohen-Macaulay closed graph cut set properties connected components after removing cut set intervals

returned_results.slogan: If a graph G has a Cohen-Macaulay ideal and a cut vertex v such that the ideal of G without v is also Cohen-Macaulay, then the ideal of the graph formed by removing v from the closed neighborhood of v is Cohen-Macaulay.
returned_results.name: Proposition 3.9

returned_results.slogan: Every non-empty cut set in a connected accessible graph with at least two cut vertices contains a cut vertex. The graph formed by the cut vertices is connected. Every vertex in the graph is adjacent to a cut vertex. These properties also hold if the graph's edge ideal is Cohen-Macaulay.
returned_results.name: Theorem 4.12

returned_results.slogan: Removing an edge from a graph preserves the Cohen-Macaulay property under certain conditions. The graph after removal must be Cohen-Macaulay. Additionally, the intersection of the variety with certain sets must have codimension at least two for all relevant partitions. These conditions ensure the original graph's variety remains Cohen-Macaulay.
returned_results.name: Lemma 6.6

returned_results.slogan: A connected graph with exactly one cut vertex and two components after removal is accessible only if it is the cone over the disjoint union of those components, and both components are accessible. If the graph's cover ideal is Cohen-Macaulay, then the cover ideals of both components are also Cohen-Macaulay.
returned_results.name: Lemma 4.9

returned_results.slogan: An indecomposable closed graph with two connected cut sets of sufficient size and separation, and no smaller connected cut set between them, implies that the ring S over J_G is not sequentially Cohen-Macaulay. The cut sets must each have at least two vertices not in the other. The absence of a shorter connected cut set in the interval is a key condition. This result links graph structure to algebraic properties of the associated ring.
returned_results.name: Proposition 2.3

returned_results.slogan: If the graph G has a Cohen-Macaulay ideal, then for any vertex v in G, the ideal of the graph after deleting v is also Cohen-Macaulay.
returned_results.name: Proposition 3.2

returned_results.slogan: Let G be a closed graph. The ideal I_G is Cohen-Macaulay. The dimension of the quotient ring S divided by I_G equals one plus the number of connected components of G.
returned_results.name: Corollary 1.3

returned_results.slogan: A Cohen-Macaulay complex remains connected even after removing a subset of codimension one. This means the complex does not separate into disjoint parts when such a subset is removed. The property holds for all complexes satisfying the Cohen-Macaulay condition.
returned_results.name: Lemma 3.2 ({\cite[Lemma 9.1.12]{MR2724673}})

returned_results.slogan: If the ideal is radical and all minimal primes yield Cohen-Macaulay quotient rings, then for any set of isolated vertices in the second graph, removing those vertices from the first graph does not disconnect it.
returned_results.name: Theorem 2.15

returned_results.slogan: A graph is Cohen-Macaulay if and only if, for every vertex, the set of neighbors that are not adjacent to each other forms a complete graph.
returned_results.name: Corollary 2.7

trajectory.query: closed graph Cohen-Macaulay characterization maximal cliques leaf order consecutive intervals

returned_results.slogan: A connected graph on n labeled vertices that is closed under a given labeling has several equivalent properties. The ideal J_G is unmixed if and only if it is Cohen-Macaulay. The initial ideal of J_G is also Cohen-Macaulay under the same conditions. The graph must satisfy a closure condition on edges and have facets arranged in a specific leaf order with consecutive integer intervals.
returned_results.name: Theorem 3.1

returned_results.slogan: A closed graph G has maximal cliques that are intervals. These intervals are arranged such that the end of one equals the start of the next. For such a graph, the Betti numbers of the edge ideal and its reverse lexicographic initial ideal are equal. This equality holds for all indices i and j.
returned_results.name: Proposition 1.1

returned_results.slogan: For a connected graph on n vertices that is closed with respect to a given labeling, several properties are equivalent. The binomial edge ideal is unmixed if and only if it is Cohen-Macaulay. The initial ideal is also Cohen-Macaulay under the same conditions. The graph must satisfy a specific closure condition on edges, and its clique complex facets form intervals in a leaf order.
returned_results.name: Theorem 1.4

returned_results.slogan: A finite bipartite graph with equally sized parts and specific edge conditions is Cohen-Macaulay if and only if a certain closure property holds. If edges exist from x_i to y_j and from x_j to y_k with i less than j less than k, then an edge must also exist from x_i to y_k. This condition ensures the graph satisfies the Cohen-Macaulay property. The theorem provides a combinatorial characterization for such graphs.
returned_results.name: Theorem 3.4

returned_results.slogan: The unmixed property of the ideal J_G1,G2 is equivalent to the existence of a specific leaf order on the facets of the clique complex of G2. This leaf order requires intervals with consecutive integers and a fixed gap condition between them. The depth of the quotient ring S over J_G1,G2 is given by a formula involving n, m, and the number of facets r. The ring is Cohen-Macaulay exactly when G2 is a complete graph.
returned_results.name: Theorem 4.4

returned_results.slogan: A graph G on n vertices is closed if and only if it has a labeling where all facets of its independence complex are intervals of consecutive integers. When these conditions are met, the facets can be ordered by their minimum elements. This ordering forms a leaf order for the independence complex.
returned_results.name: Theorem 3.2

returned_results.slogan: An indecomposable closed graph has a sequentially Cohen-Macaulay binomial edge ideal if and only if there exists an index such that the upper endpoints of the facets form an arithmetic sequence from that index onward, and the lower endpoints form an arithmetic sequence up to that index. The graph's clique complex is generated by a specific set of intervals. The conditions on the endpoints are both necessary and sufficient for the ideal to be sequentially Cohen-Macaulay.
returned_results.name: Theorem 2.2

returned_results.slogan: A graph on n vertices is closed if and only if it has a labeling where all facets of its independence complex are intervals. If these conditions hold and the facets are ordered by increasing minimum element, that ordering forms a leaf order for the independence complex.
returned_results.name: Theorem 2.1

returned_results.slogan: A graph G on n vertices is closed if and only if it can be labeled so that all facets of its independence complex are intervals. When these conditions hold, ordering the facets by increasing minimum vertex gives a leaf order of the independence complex.
returned_results.name: Theorem 2.2

returned_results.slogan: A graph G on n vertices is closed if and only if the generators of its binomial edge ideal form a Gröbner basis under lex order. This is also equivalent to the facets of its clique complex being intervals. These intervals can be ordered so that the first starts at 1, the last ends at n, and the starting points are strictly increasing.
returned_results.name: Theorem 1.2

trajectory.query: for Cohen-Macaulay closed graph cut sets are intervals or unions of endpoints D_S dominating vertices formula components after deleting S

returned_results.slogan: For a Cohen-Macaulay closed graph, the v-number of the binomial edge ideal corresponding to any cut set S equals twice the size of S plus the number of dominating vertices in S.
returned_results.name: Theorem 3.4

returned_results.slogan: If a graph G has a Cohen-Macaulay ideal and a cut vertex v such that the ideal of G without v is also Cohen-Macaulay, then the ideal of the graph formed by removing v from the closed neighborhood of v is Cohen-Macaulay.
returned_results.name: Proposition 3.9

returned_results.slogan: Every non-empty cut set in a connected accessible graph with at least two cut vertices contains a cut vertex. The graph formed by the cut vertices is connected. Every vertex in the graph is adjacent to a cut vertex. These properties also hold if the graph's edge ideal is Cohen-Macaulay.
returned_results.name: Theorem 4.12

returned_results.slogan: An indecomposable closed graph with two connected cut sets of sufficient size and separation, and no smaller connected cut set between them, implies that the ring S over J_G is not sequentially Cohen-Macaulay. The cut sets must each have at least two vertices not in the other. The absence of a shorter connected cut set in the interval is a key condition. This result links graph structure to algebraic properties of the associated ring.
returned_results.name: Proposition 2.3

returned_results.slogan: If D_H is a Cohen-Macaulay graph, then D_G is also Cohen-Macaulay. Additionally, if every vertex v in D_F adjacent to any x_j from s+1 to k has an edge to x_j in D_G, then D_F is Cohen-Macaulay as well.
returned_results.name: Proposition 3.5

returned_results.slogan: If a graph D_H is Cohen-Macaulay, and for every vertex v in D_F adjacent to any x_j from index s+1 to k, the edge (v, x_j) is present in graph D_G, then D_F is also a Cohen-Macaulay graph.
returned_results.name: Proposition 3.11

returned_results.slogan: A non-empty subset W of a connected closed graph is a cut set if and only if it can be written as a union of connected cut sets with indices strictly separated by at least one integer. The dimension of the quotient ring S divided by the prime ideal P_W of G is at most n plus one. This dimension equals n plus one exactly when each connected cut set in the union consists of a single vertex.
returned_results.name: Proposition 1.4

returned_results.slogan: Removing a vertex set S from a simple graph G results in a chordal graph. Adding a clique on S to G produces a graph that is sequentially Cohen-Macaulay.
returned_results.name: Theorem 3.2

returned_results.slogan: If D_H is a Cohen-Macaulay graph, then both D_F and D_G are also Cohen-Macaulay graphs.
returned_results.name: Proposition 3.2

returned_results.slogan: For a Cohen-Macaulay closed graph G, the colon ideal of J_G with respect to the product f_S f_{D_S} equals the prime ideal P_S.
returned_results.name: Lemma 3.2

trajectory.query: colon ideal (J_G : g) = P_S existence for cut set S closed graph lex order initial ideal

returned_results.slogan: The colon ideal of the first i minus one generators with the i-th generator equals the ideal generated by the variables t sub r for all r in the set S sub i. returned_results.slogan: For a simple graph G on r vertices, let S be a polynomial ring and J_G the associated binomial edge ideal. If the initial ideal of J_G under lex order is such that its symbolic powers equal its ordinary powers for all n, then the same holds for J_G itself. In particular, if G is a closed graph, then the symbolic and ordinary powers of J_G coincide for all nonnegative integers n.
returned_results.name: Corollary 4.13 (\cite [Theorem 3.3 and Corollary 3.5]{EHBEI})

returned_results.slogan: For a simple graph G with edge ideal I and a natural number s, consider an ideal J defined by I raised to s and divided by a product of s minus one edges. If the first edge is a leaf of G, then J equals I raised to s minus one divided by the product of the remaining edges. If a vertex w is not in the closed neighborhood of the edges, then the colon ideal J colon w equals the ideal of the graph minus the closed neighborhood of w raised to s and divided by the product of edges, plus the neighbors of w. If w is in the closed neighborhood of the first edge, then J colon w equals an ideal involving a smaller power and a subset of edges, plus the neighbors of w in a derived graph.

returned_results.slogan: The ideal J_G is radical. The ideal J_G equals the intersection of all P_T(G) over all subsets T. A prime ideal P_T(G) is a minimal prime of J_G if and only if T is empty or has the cut point property.
returned_results.name: Theorem 2.1

returned_results.slogan: Given a graph G with an edge x_i x_j, for any integer s between 1 and the height of I(G) minus 1, the colon ideal of the (s+1)-th symbolic power of I(G) with respect to x_i x_j equals the intersection of the colon ideals of the s-th symbolic powers of I(G-x_j) with respect to x_i and I(G-x_i) with respect to x_j.
returned_results.name: Lemma 6.4

returned_results.slogan: For a graph G and a positive integer s at most one less than the cover ideal's initial degree, the monomials in the cover ideal's s-th power can be ordered. returned_results.slogan: The regularity of the binomial edge ideal for the join of two disjoint graphs equals the maximum of the regularities of the individual ideals or three. returned_results.name: Theorem 2.1

returned_results.slogan: The regularity of the edge ideal of a graph formed by gluing two fan graphs depends on a parameter t and the sizes of certain subsets. If t is at most one, the regularity equals the sum of the regularities of the two fan graphs minus t. If t equals two and one subset has size one less than its corresponding n, the regularity is the sum minus one. If t equals two and both subsets have size equal to their corresponding n, the regularity is the sum minus two.
returned_results.name: Theorem 3.8

returned_results.slogan: The regularity of the binomial edge ideal of a graph formed by joining two graphs is at most n minus one, provided the graph is not a path on two or three vertices.
returned_results.name: Corollary 3.24

returned_results.slogan: The depth of the binomial edge ideal for a graph formed by attaching two graphs at a common free vertex equals the sum of the depths of the ideals for each graph minus two. This result holds when the graphs are on disjoint vertex sets and are joined by identifying a vertex that is free in both. The polynomial rings correspond to the vertex sets of the graphs over a field.
returned_results.name: Proposition 2.5

returned_results.slogan: The regularity of the edge ideal for a graph formed by gluing two fan graphs depends on a parameter t and the sizes of the sets W_i. If t is at most one, the regularity equals the sum of the regularities of the individual fan graphs. If t equals two and each W_i has size n_i minus one, the regularity is again the sum. If t equals two and some W_i has size n_i, the regularity is one less than the sum.
returned_results.name: Theorem 3.10

returned_results.slogan: The regularity of the binomial edge ideal of a connected graph equals the sum of the regularities of the binomial edge ideals of its connected components.
returned_results.name: Corollary 3.10

returned_results.slogan: The regularity of the quotient ring for a k-fan graph of a complete graph is at least k plus one. This holds for complete graphs with at least two vertices. The k-fan graph is constructed from the complete graph on a specified vertex set. The result provides a lower bound on the Castelnuovo-Mumford regularity.
returned_results.name: Corollary 3.5

returned_results.slogan: The regularity of the ring S over J_G for a k-fan graph of the complete graph on n vertices is at most the number of maximal cliques in the graph. If for every fan and every index, the integer a sub i comma j is greater than j plus one, then the regularity equals the number of maximal cliques.
returned_results.name: Theorem 3.3

returned_results.slogan: The regularity of the edge ideal of a k-fan graph of a complete graph depends on the size of a subset W and the number of parts in its partition with at least two elements. If the subset has size at least n minus one and each part has at least two elements, the regularity equals the number of parts with two or more elements. Otherwise, the regularity is one more than that number.
returned_results.name: Theorem 2.8

returned_results.slogan: The regularity of the quotient ring S over J_G for a k-pure fan graph of the complete graph on n vertices equals k plus one. This holds when n is at least two.
returned_results.name: Theorem 3.4

returned_results.slogan: The regularity of the graph's binomial edge ideal equals the sum of the regularities of the binomial edge ideals for two smaller fan graphs. Each of these smaller graphs is obtained by reducing the number of vertices by one. The result is always six.

returned_results.slogan: For graphs formed by composing multiple fan graphs with a base graph H, the Castelnuovo-Mumford regularity of the quotient ring equals the sum of the regularities of smaller fan graphs and the regularity of the base graph after removing two specific vertices. The base graph H is either a fan graph or a generalized fan graph built from a complete graph. The composition requires at least two fan graphs, each with at least three vertices. The regularity formula holds under specific conditions on the vertex connections and the structure of H.

returned_results.slogan: The regularity of the ring modulo the binomial edge ideal of a graph formed by gluing two graphs at a vertex equals the sum of the regularities of the ideals of the two modified graphs. returned_results.slogan: The regularity of the edge ideal of a graph formed by clique-sums of bipartite graphs and odd cycles depends on a parameter k. returned_results.slogan: For a doubly Cohen-Macaulay graph G, the regularity of the k-th symbolic power of its cover ideal equals k times the degree of the cover ideal, for all positive integers k.

returned_results.name: Corollary 3.10

returned_results.slogan: If two connected graphs have unmixed binomial edge ideals, then their join product also has an unmixed binomial edge ideal exactly when both graphs are complete.

returned_results.slogan: The join of a vertex with a disconnected graph, where the graph splits into two connected parts, results in a Cohen-Macaulay ideal. returned_results.slogan: The regularity of the quotient ring by the binomial edge ideal of a graph equals the regularity of the quotient by its initial ideal, and both are equal to the graph's chordal length.

If there is a cutset T not containing v such that the v-number equals the T-v-number, then the v-number of the graph with v removed is at most that of G. If there is a cutset T containing v with the same equality, then the v-number of the graph with v deleted is at most that of G.

trajectory.query: stringy Euler characteristic of a Q-Gorenstein toric variety equals volume of the shed associated to the fan

returned_results.slogan: For any normal Q-Gorenstein toric variety defined by a fan, the stringy Euler number equals the volume of the fan. This number is always an integer.
returned_results.name: Proposition

returned_results.slogan: For a Q-Gorenstein toric variety from a fan, the total stringy Chern class is a sum over all cones in the fan. Each term multiplies a volume factor by the class of the corresponding torus orbit closure. The volume factor is k factorial times the k-dimensional volume of a specific lattice polytope. This polytope is the convex hull of the origin and the primitive generators of the one-dimensional faces of the cone.
returned_results.name: Theorem 3.2

returned_results.slogan: The stringy Euler number of a generic semiample divisor on a projective Q-Gorenstein toric variety is expressed as a sum over cones in the fan. This sum involves alternating signs and the volumes of cones and corresponding polytope faces. When the divisor class equals the first Chern class of the variety, the summation range changes and the formula simplifies. The result is given in terms of combinatorial data from the fan and associated polytope.
returned_results.name: Corollary 3.6

returned_results.slogan: The intersection of a torus-invariant divisor with the stringy Chern class of a projective toric variety equals a sum over codimension-one cones. Each term in the sum is the product of a volume factor and a rational number associated with the divisor. The rational number depends on the divisor and the cone. This formula holds for Q-Gorenstein toric varieties.
returned_results.name: Proposition 3.4

returned_results.slogan: The stringy E-function of a projective Q-Gorenstein toric variety can be expressed as a finite sum over cones in a simplicial subdivision of its fan. This sum involves terms based on the dimension of each cone and lattice points in the relative interior of a parallelepiped. The function can also be written as a finite sum with nonnegative integer coefficients that are symmetric and satisfy specific boundary conditions. These coefficients are indexed by rational numbers determined by the Gorenstein index of the variety.
returned_results.name: Proposition 4.1

returned_results.slogan: The stringy Euler number of a Calabi-Yau complete intersection in a Gorenstein toric Fano variety is given by a combinatorial formula. This formula sums over faces of a Gorenstein polytope associated with the variety. The terms involve the volumes of faces and their duals, along with binomial coefficients and alternating signs. The expression depends on the dimension of the variety and the index of the polytope.
returned_results.name: Theorem 5.7

returned_results.slogan: For a d-dimensional Q-Gorenstein toric variety X from a fan Sigma, the k-th stringy Chern class is given by summing over all k-dimensional cones in the fan. Each term multiplies a weight v(sigma) by the class of the orbit closure corresponding to the cone. The result holds for integers k between 0 and d inclusive.
returned_results.name: Corollary 3.3

returned_results.slogan: The string-theoretic Euler number of a projective toric variety is given by the factorial of the dimension multiplied by the volume of the dual polytope.
returned_results.name: Corollary

returned_results.slogan: The stringy Euler number of a complete intersection of generic semiample divisors in a projective toric variety is expressed as a combinatorial sum. The formula involves summing over cones in the fan and volumes of associated polytopes. It includes alternating signs and binomial coefficients. The result depends on the dimension of the variety and the number of intersecting divisors.
returned_results.name: Corollary 3.7

returned_results.slogan: The stringy E-function of a Gorenstein complete toric variety or a nondegenerate complete intersection of Cartier hypersurfaces in such a variety equals a sum over its torus orbit stratification. Each term in the sum is the product of the intersection E-function of the closure of a stratum and a function depending on the Gorenstein cone of the singularity along that stratum. The function S tilde is evaluated at the product of the variables u and v. This formula expresses the global invariant in terms of contributions from the singularities along each stratum.
returned_results.name: Theorem

returned_results.name: Lemma 4.2

returned_results.slogan: The map sending a divisor to its Euler characteristic defines an isomorphism between the group of divisors and the Grothendieck group. This isomorphism connects the divisor class group to the K zero group of the module. The groups are structurally identical under this mapping.

returned_results.slogan: The Euler characteristic of the n-th K-theory sheaf for the product of a g-dimensional abelian variety with an r-dimensional smooth quasi-projective variety is invariant under replacing the abelian variety with another g-dimensional abelian variety. This equality holds regardless of the specific abelian varieties chosen. The result applies to varieties of the stated dimensions.

returned_results.slogan: The equality holds in the Grothendieck group K sub I zero. The derived pushforwards with compact support of the constant sheaf on the diagonal are compared. The invariants under the group G are taken at two different geometric points. The result is the same regardless of the choice of base scheme or point.

returned_results.slogan: The K-group of a graded finite rank Hilbert module equals its Euler characteristic.
returned_results.name: Theorem 8.2 (Arveson 2000)

returned_results.slogan: The assignment mapping an object to its zero complex induces an isomorphism between the Grothendieck group of an exact category and a defined variant. The Euler characteristic is computed as an alternating sum of the classes of its terms in the Grothendieck group. This establishes a natural equivalence between these two groups.

returned_results.slogan: The equivalence class of a triple in the derived category of a functor equals the image of its Euler characteristic under the inclusion map. This identity holds within the Grothendieck group of the derived category. The result expresses a relation in K-theory for derived categories.

returned_results.slogan: An equality holds in the K zero group of p adic group rings. The homomorphism acts on a product of an invariant and a module of differentials.

returned_results.slogan: The Grothendieck group of the fixed subcategory under the Galois group action equals the fixed part of the Grothendieck group of the original category. This holds when the Galois group acts on the category associated to a certain object. The result relates equivariant K-theory to invariants under group actions. It expresses a compatibility between group actions and K-zero groups.

returned_results.slogan: If a crepant resolution exists from Y to the quotient of complex n-space by a finite group G, then the Euler number of Y equals the number of conjugacy classes in G.
returned_results.name: Theorem 1.1

returned_results.slogan: The stringy Chern class of X equals the sum over conjugacy classes of G of the pushforward of the Chern-Schwartz-MacPherson class of the quotient of the fixed locus by the centralizer. This identity holds in the Chow group of X.
returned_results.name: Theorem 6.3

returned_results.slogan: For a normal projective Q-Gorenstein variety with log-terminal singularities and a generic semiample Cartier divisor, the stringy Euler number of the divisor equals a signed sum of products of powers of the divisor class with stringy Chern classes of the variety. When the divisor class equals the first Chern class of the variety, the divisor has trivial anticanonical class and the formula simplifies by excluding the last two terms.
returned_results.name: Corollary 1.4

returned_results.slogan: The stringy Chern class integral of a proper variety with log-terminal singularities equals its stringy Euler number.
returned_results.name: Proposition 4.4

returned_results.slogan: A finite subgroup of the special linear group over complex numbers has a crepant resolution of its quotient variety. The topological Euler characteristic of this resolution equals the number of conjugacy classes in the group. This equality holds for such resolutions of affine space quotients by finite subgroups.
returned_results.name: Theorem 1.1 (\cite{Bat})

returned_results.slogan: For a finite subgroup G of SL(n, C), if the quotient space X equals C^n divided by G has a crepant resolution Y mapping to X, then the rational cohomology of Y has a basis of algebraic cycles. These cycles correspond one-to-one with the conjugacy classes of G. Consequently, the Euler number of Y equals the number of conjugacy classes in G.
returned_results.name: Theorem 1.2 (Batyrev)

trajectory.query: number of irreducible representations equals number of conjugacy classes of a finite group

returned_results.slogan: The number of irreducible representations of a finite group equals the number of conjugacy classes in that group.
returned_results.name: Corollary 1.13

returned_results.slogan: The number of irreducible representations of a group equals the number of its conjugacy classes. This holds for any finite group.
returned_results.name: Proposition 1.2.2.1

returned_results.slogan: The number of irreducible representations of a group equals the number of its conjugacy classes.
returned_results.name: Theorem 3.1.13 ({see \cite [Section 2.2]{MR1153249}})

returned_results.slogan: A finite group has a number of irreducible representations equal to the number of its conjugacy classes. This count is exact and applies to all finite groups. The representations are over the complex numbers. This is a fundamental result in representation theory.
returned_results.name: Proposition 2

returned_results.slogan: The number of nonisomorphic irreducible representations of a finite group equals the number of its distinct conjugacy classes. This is a fundamental result in representation theory. It establishes a key connection between group structure and its representations. The theorem holds for all finite groups.
returned_results.name: Theorem 2.17

returned_results.slogan: The number of inequivalent irreducible representations of a finite group equals the number of its conjugacy classes. This means there is a one-to-one correspondence between these two sets. The result holds for any finite group over an algebraically closed field. It is a fundamental fact in representation theory.
returned_results.name: Theorem 2.21

returned_results.slogan: The number of irreducible representations of a finite group equals the number of conjugacy classes in the group. The sum of the squares of the degrees of all irreducible representations equals the order of the group. This holds for any finite group.
returned_results.name: Theorem 3.1

returned_results.slogan: The number of conjugacy classes in a group equals the number of its irreducible representations. This holds for finite groups over an algebraically closed field. Each conjugacy class corresponds to a distinct irreducible character. The result is fundamental in character theory.
returned_results.name: Theorem 2.2

returned_results.slogan: The number of irreducible representations of a finite group equals the number of its conjugacy classes. This holds for representations over an algebraically closed field where the characteristic does not divide the group order. Each conjugacy class corresponds to exactly one irreducible representation. This is a fundamental result in representation theory.
returned_results.name: Theorem 11.4 (Main Theorem)

returned_results.slogan: A finite group has the same number of irreducible complex representations as conjugacy classes. The representations are considered up to equivalence. This count is a fundamental property of finite groups.
returned_results.name: Proposition 0.1 (Classical)

trajectory.query: NCCR of quotient singularity indecomposable summands correspond to irreducible representations McKay

returned_results.slogan: For a subgroup of SL acting on a two-dimensional space, four sets are in one-to-one correspondence: irreducible components of the exceptional divisor, nontrivial irreducible representations, nontrivial indecomposable Cohen-Macaulay modules, and nontrivial indecomposable summands of the ring extension. The multiplicity of each divisor component equals the dimension of its corresponding representation and the multiplicity of its corresponding module. The McKay quiver and Auslander-Reiten quiver coincide. The dual resolution graph is obtained by removing the trivial representation vertex and collapsing two-cycles into edges.
returned_results.name: Theorem 2.20 (Classical McKay correspondence)

returned_results.slogan: A two-dimensional complete local normal domain over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero is a quotient singularity from a finite group acting on a power series ring if and only if it has a steady noncommutative crepant resolution. This is also equivalent to the ring having any noncommutative crepant resolution. Another equivalent condition is that there are only finitely many isomorphism classes of indecomposable maximal Cohen-Macaulay modules. In this situation, all noncommutative crepant resolutions are steady and correspond to additive generators of the category of maximal Cohen-Macaulay modules.
returned_results.name: Proposition 4.2

returned_results.slogan: A two-dimensional complete local normal domain over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero is a quotient singularity from a finite group acting on a power series ring if and only if it has a steady noncommutative crepant resolution. This is also equivalent to having a semi-steady noncommutative crepant resolution, or any noncommutative crepant resolution. Furthermore, these conditions are equivalent to the ring having only finitely many non-isomorphic indecomposable maximal Cohen-Macaulay modules. When these hold, modules providing noncommutative crepant resolutions are additive generators of the category of maximal Cohen-Macaulay modules.
returned_results.name: Proposition 2.9

returned_results.slogan: For an algebraically closed field and a finite linearly reductive subgroup scheme of SL2, the Ito-Nakamura resolution of the Klein singularity has an exceptional divisor. The irreducible components of this divisor correspond bijectively to the nontrivial simple representations of the group. The intersection numbers of these components equal the entries of the McKay graph adjacency matrix. This yields a bijection between the McKay graph and the dual resolution graph of the singularity.
returned_results.name: Theorem 5.3

returned_results.slogan: Given a complete set of non-isomorphic irreducible representations of a group over a field, the corresponding invariant modules form a complete set of non-isomorphic indecomposable maximal Cohen-Macaulay modules over the invariant ring. For any representation decomposing as a direct sum of irreducible components with multiplicities, the associated invariant module decomposes similarly into the corresponding indecomposable modules with the same multiplicities.
returned_results.name: Corollary 2.5

returned_results.slogan: The minimal resolution of an A_n surface singularity maps to the quotient of the complex plane by a cyclic group. Each irreducible component of the fiber over zero corresponds to a vertex in the quiver via the McKay correspondence. Under this process, the component associated to a given vertex contracts to the simple module at that vertex over the preprojective algebra. This establishes a geometric realization of the module structure.
returned_results.name: Corollary 4.6

returned_results.slogan: A noncommutative isolated singularity has the property that every nonprojective indecomposable maximal Cohen-Macaulay module is isomorphic to a direct summand of a fixed module M, possibly after shifting degrees.
returned_results.name: Lemma 4.26

returned_results.slogan: For a normal Gorenstein surface singularity, consider a special module without free direct factors and its associated module on a resolution. There are natural bijections between the indecomposable summands of the original module and those of its associated module. These also correspond bijectively to the irreducible components of the supports of two constructed objects from given generic sections.
returned_results.name: Proposition 5.15

returned_results.slogan: For a true reflection group G, the quotient algebra A over AeA is isomorphic to the endomorphism ring of S over J modulo the discriminant. Indecomposable projective modules over this quotient correspond to nontrivial irreducible G-representations and to direct summands of S over J modulo the discriminant. This quotient algebra forms a noncommutative resolution of singularities for the discriminant ring. The global dimension of this resolution is the dimension of R plus one when G is not the group of order two.
returned_results.name: Theorem (=Thm.~ \ref{Thm:main} and Corollaries)

returned_results.slogan: For a finite subgroup G of SL(2,k) over an algebraically closed field k of characteristic not 2, 3, or 5, the exceptional curves in the minimal resolution of the quotient singularity correspond bijectively to the irreducible representations of G and to the indecomposable maximal Cohen-Macaulay modules over the invariant ring. The dual graph of the resolution is isomorphic to the McKay quiver with the trivial vertex removed and opposed arrows replaced by edges. This graph is an ADE Coxeter-Dynkin diagram. The possible diagrams are of types A_n, D_n, E_6, E_7, or E_8.
returned_results.name: Theorem J.6 (Classical McKay Correspondence)

Additionally, if all edges from a vertex point into the set, then that vertex itself is included. This property holds for any ideal within the Leavitt path algebra.

returned_results.slogan: An ideal I in a Leavitt path algebra L can be written as the sum of an ideal generated by hereditary saturated sets and ideals generated by polynomials applied to cycles without exits. The intersection of the ideal generated by hereditary saturated sets with the set of vertices equals the hereditary saturated set itself. For any ideal J in L, the product ideals I times J and J times I are equal.

returned_results.slogan: A homology sphere with the weak Lefschetz property over a field satisfies the g-conjecture. A linear form is a weak Lefschetz element if multiplication by it is surjective in a certain degree. This surjectivity condition is equivalent to injectivity in a complementary degree. These conditions are defined on the quotient of the face ring by a linear system of parameters.
returned_results.name: Proposition 2.6

returned_results.slogan: The h-vector of a certain complex satisfies a symmetry relation. For dimensions at least four, the first three g-numbers form an M-vector. If all vertex links have the weak Lefschetz property, then the entire g-vector up to the floor of half the dimension is an M-vector.
returned_results.name: Theorem 5.1

returned_results.slogan: A (d-1)-dimensional Gorenstein star complex has the weak Lefschetz property exactly when the size of its U-vector matches the g-vector for indices up to half the dimension and is zero beyond that. If the complex has the strong Lefschetz property, a monomial from a certain ring lies in the Lefschetz set if and only if its reduced part is in the U-vector and its exponent satisfies an inequality. The inequality requires the exponent to be at least twice the degree of the reduced monomial minus the dimension. These conditions characterize the Lefschetz properties for such complexes.
returned_results.name: Lemma 3.4

returned_results.slogan: The g-vector of a simplicial complex is always nonnegative.
returned_results.name: Corollary 3.2

returned_results.slogan: A simplicial complex Delta that is a connected orientable homology manifold without boundary over a field F has the weak Lefschetz property for its face ring if and only if the face ring of the stellar subdivision of Delta at a face sigma also has the weak Lefschetz property. This equivalence holds when the dimension of sigma is greater than half the dimension of Delta. The result connects the Lefschetz property of the original complex to that of its subdivision at a sufficiently large face.
returned_results.name: Theorem 4.3

returned_results.slogan: The squarefree reduction of the Stanley-Reisner ideal of a simplicial complex has the weak Lefschetz property in characteristic zero and degree i if and only if one of two conditions is met. The first condition requires that the number of i minus one-dimensional faces is at most the number of i-dimensional faces, and a certain multiplicity is positive. The second condition requires that the number of i-dimensional faces is at most the number of i minus one-dimensional faces, and a different multiplicity is positive. These multiplicities are defined with respect to the ideal and its relation to the complex.
returned_results.name: Theorem 52 (\textbf{WLP in characteristic zero and mixed multiplicities})

returned_results.slogan: A simplicial complex with the weak Lefschetz property in characteristic zero and degree i, and with f_{i-1} less than or equal to f_i, also has the weak Lefschetz property in degree i and characteristic p under a specific condition. The condition depends on a prime number p not dividing a certain integer expression. This expression involves a greatest common divisor computed over all subsets of generators of the i-th incidence ideal with size f_{i-1}. The integer includes a factor of i+1 multiplied by this gcd.
returned_results.name: Theorem 46 (\textbf{WLP in positive characteristics and mixed multiplicities})

returned_results.slogan: The g-theorem characterizes the possible g-vectors of simplicial d-polytopes. A vector is a valid g-vector if and only if it equals the Hilbert function of a finitely generated graded commutative algebra generated in degree one. The first component of the vector must be one. All other components up to half the dimension must be non-negative.
returned_results.name: Theorem 2.1

returned_results.slogan: If gamma is an f-vector of a simplicial complex, then g is also an f-vector of a simplicial complex.

returned_results.slogan: The h-vector and g-vector of a simplicial complex are f-vectors under several conditions. These include if the complex is the barycentric subdivision of a boolean complex with symmetric and nonnegative h-vector, such as a simplicial sphere. They also hold if the complex is a Coxeter complex or the dual complex of an associahedron or cyclohedron. Additionally, the property applies to flag homology spheres where the first gamma invariant is at most three.
