returned_results.slogan: Given a sequence of functions satisfying a prescribed equation with exponents approaching a critical value and blowing up, the blow-up points are isolated, simple, and located in a specific subset of the sphere. The number and positions of these points satisfy a separation condition and a nonnegative mass property. Certain limits involving the functions and their maxima exist and are finite. These limits relate to the Laplacian of a given function when there is one blow-up point, and to a system of equations involving a mass matrix when there are multiple points. The positivity of these limits is equivalent to the strict positivity of the mass matrix's least eigenvalue.
returned_results.name: Theorem 2.1

returned_results.slogan: The local mass of a sequence of blow-up solutions for the system is given by an affine Toda mass vector. This vector equals a specific element from a certain set of admissible masses, up to an even integer multiple. The integer multiples are added component-wise to each entry of the admissible mass vector. The result holds for all indices in the index set.

returned_results.slogan: As time approaches zero from below, the squared magnitude of the solution converges weakly to a sum of Dirac masses, each with mass equal to the squared L2 norm of Q, located at specific points. The solution itself converges to zero in L2 norm on the real line excluding small neighborhoods around these points. The total squared L2 norm of the solution is equal to K times the squared L2 norm of Q. This behavior describes a mass quantization phenomenon at the blow-up time.

returned_results.name: Proposition 4.2

returned_results.slogan: The mass of the conformal blow-up metric at a point is bounded above by a negative fraction involving the Laplacian and the value of a function at that point. This inequality holds under a given condition without assuming the metrics are conformal normal. If a certain sequence is identically zero, the equality holds exactly. The equality case provides a precise formula for the mass.
returned_results.name: Proposition 4.11

returned_results.slogan: A solution that blows up at a finite time concentrates a minimal amount of mass. This concentration occurs at specific points in space and time approaching the blow-up time. The minimal mass is at least the squared L2 norm of a fixed function Q on the plane. This holds for any positive radius around the concentration points.
returned_results.name: Theorem 2

returned_results.slogan: A blow-up solution sequence converges to a function away from the blow-up point. The limit function satisfies a partial differential equation involving a Laplacian and Dirac delta terms. The equation includes parameters from natural numbers and a total mass condition. The integral of the exponential term converges to a scaled version of the limit's integral.
returned_results.name: Theorem 1.1

trajectory.query: description of low sublevels functional J_rho concentration at points and scales topological join barycenter sets

returned_results.slogan: The minimum value of the functional J over the set D_rho is equal to the minimum among all critical points of J restricted to D_rho. This holds under the assumptions labeled F0 through F2, J2, and equation rho. The result characterizes the minimal energy level in terms of stationary points on the constraint set.
returned_results.name: Proposition 1.4

returned_results.slogan: The functional J is lower semi-continuous and has compact level sets. For any non-negative r, the set of points where J is at most r is compact.
returned_results.name: Proposition 4.2

returned_results.slogan: For any function u in the intersection of the set N_epsilon and the sublevel set J to the power m_e plus delta, with sufficiently small epsilon and delta, the barycenter beta of u lies in the three rho neighborhood of the boundary of M.
returned_results.name: Proposition 14

returned_results.slogan: Given a bounded Palais-Smale sequence for the functional J_rho at a nonnegative level, a subsequence converges to some function u in the space X. The limit of J_rho applied to the sequence minus u equals the original level minus J_rho of u. The derivative of J_rho applied to the sequence minus u converges to zero in X. These results hold under the condition that rho is nonnegative and less than a specific ratio.
returned_results.name: Lemma 4.2

returned_results.slogan: For any small positive epsilon and r, there exists a large constant L such that if a function u in H^1 has energy J_rho_alpha(u) at most -L, then most of the weighted exponential of 2u concentrates near certain points. These points include some within 2r of specified locations p_i and others at least 2r away from all p_i. The concentration occurs in balls of radius r around these points, covering a fraction of at least 1 minus epsilon of the total integral.
returned_results.name: Lemma 3.11

returned_results.slogan: A Cerami sequence exists at level c_rho for a functional J_rho that is continuously differentiable and satisfies certain conditions. The value c_rho is defined as an infimum over paths in a specified set Gamma. Under an additional assumption, c_rho is bounded above by the infimum of J_rho over a set N_rho. If c_rho is at least the value of J_rho at some critical point, then c_rho equals the infimum of J_rho over N_rho.
returned_results.name: Theorem 3.1

returned_results.slogan: For any sufficiently small positive epsilon and r, there exists a positive L such that if u is in the sublevel set J_rho to minus L, then for at least one index i, there is a subset J of Sigma with a certain chi characteristic bounded by rho_i. The integral of f_i,u over the union of balls of radius r around points in J_i is at least one minus epsilon.
returned_results.name: Lemma

returned_results.slogan: Let F satisfy conditions Fp, F0, and F1. There exists a threshold value rho-bar such that for all rho greater than rho-bar, there is a function u-bar in H1 with L2 norm equal to rho that minimizes the functional J over all such functions. This minimizer u-bar is positive and radially symmetric. Additionally, there exists a negative constant lambda such that u-bar and lambda together solve the equation.
returned_results.name: Theorem 2

returned_results.slogan: For a parameter rho in an interval between 4k pi and 4(k+1) pi with k at least 1, and for any positive epsilon and r, there exists a large constant L depending on epsilon and r. Whenever a function u in the Sobolev space H^1 has its energy J_rho(u) below negative L, then k points on the surface Sigma can be found. The exponential of 2u integrated outside balls of radius r around these points is less than epsilon times the full integral of e^(2u) over Sigma. This shows that most of the mass of e^(2u) is concentrated near these k points.
returned_results.name: Proposition 1.1 (\cite{cli1}, \cite{zind})

returned_results.slogan: The sublevel set of a functional J, consisting of all points where J is at most b, has finite genus for any real number b.
returned_results.name: Lemma 5

trajectory.query: topological join of barycenter spaces low sublevels map from join into very negative sublevels mean field equation

returned_results.slogan: For sufficiently large parameter values, the functional J evaluated at a specific test function tends to negative infinity uniformly over a certain domain. This holds under given conditions on the parameters rho one and rho two. Consequently, a related mapping sends a topological join into the sublevel set of J for any negative threshold. This implies the existence of a large parameter ensuring the mapping property.
returned_results.name: Proposition 5.2

returned_results.slogan: The space of loops with energy slightly above a critical value is homotopy equivalent to the space of loops with energy slightly below that value, with a disk attached along its boundary. The attachment uses a specific gluing map from a sphere to the lower energy loop space. This equivalence holds for a negative bundle associated with the critical point.
returned_results.name: Theorem

returned_results.slogan: For sufficiently large negative energy levels, the homotopy type of the sublevel set depends on the parameters m and m-bar. If m is at least 2 and m-bar is zero, the sublevel set has the homotopy type of the configuration space of m-1 points on M. If m is at least 2 and m-bar is at least 1, the homotopy type is that of a specific space A. If m is 1 and m-bar is at least 1, the homotopy type is a sphere of dimension m-bar minus one.
returned_results.name: Lemma 7.5

returned_results.slogan: Under certain conditions on k and k-bar, and for a sufficiently small positive eta, there exists a large constant L depending on k, k-bar, and eta. For all L at least this constant, the negative L sublevel set of the energy functional has a specific homotopy type. If k is at least 2 and k-bar is zero, it has the homotopy type of the configuration space of k minus one points on the boundary. If k is at least 2 and k-bar is at least one, it is homotopy equivalent to a certain space A sub k minus one, k-bar, and if k equals one and k-bar is at least one, it is homotopy equivalent to a sphere of dimension k-bar minus one.
returned_results.name: Lemma 4.4

returned_results.slogan: For certain ranges of the parameters rho1 and rho2, given any positive epsilon, there exists a positive L such that any function u in the sublevel set J_rho to the power of negative L satisfies that either the distance from the normalized exponential of u to the manifold M is less than epsilon, or the distance from the normalized exponential of negative a times u to M is less than epsilon. Additionally, for sufficiently large L, there is a continuous map from that sublevel set to the join of M with itself.
returned_results.name: Proposition 4.1

returned_results.slogan: For a ground state solution with negative coupling parameter beta, the integral of the product of the squared components tends to zero as beta tends to negative infinity. The solution converges strongly to a nonzero limit. Each component of the limit is a ground state solution of a separate nonlinear equation. The positivity sets of these limit functions are connected and form complementary subsets of the entire space.
returned_results.name: Theorem

returned_results.slogan: The functional tilde J lambda belongs to the space H0 and decomposes into tilde Phi lambda plus tilde Psi, where tilde Psi is the restriction of Psi to the radial Sobolev space. If tilde J lambda of u is negative, then the norm of u is less than R0 and tilde J lambda of u equals J lambda of u. Any Palais-Smale sequence for tilde J lambda at a negative level is also a Palais-Smale sequence for J lambda. A critical point of tilde J lambda within the ball of radius R0 is also a critical point of J lambda.
returned_results.name: Lemma 4.20

returned_results.slogan: Let X be a real Banach space and J be a smooth, even, real-valued function on X that is bounded below and satisfies the Palais-Smale condition, with J at zero equal to zero. For every positive integer k, assume there is a k-dimensional subspace of X and a radius such that the supremum of J on the corresponding sphere is negative. Then J has a sequence of negative critical values converging to zero.
returned_results.name: Theorem 24 ({\cite[Lemma 2.4]{Wang01}})

returned_results.slogan: Let X be a real Banach space and J be a smooth, even, bounded below function on X with J at zero equal to zero. If J satisfies the Palais-Smale condition and for each positive integer k, there is a k-dimensional subspace where the supremum of J on its sphere is negative, then J has a sequence of negative critical values converging to zero.
returned_results.name: Theorem 5.5 ({\cite[Lemma 2.4]{Wang01}})

returned_results.slogan: Under certain parameter conditions, a map is constructed from a product set or sphere into a function space. The image of this map has energy bounded above by a large negative constant. The composition of this map with a previously defined map is homotopic to the identity on the domain.
returned_results.name: Proposition

trajectory.query: macroscopic improved Moser-Trudinger inequality if two components spread over disjoint regions then coercive asymmetric sinh-Gordon

returned_results.slogan: The theorem improves the Trudinger-Moser inequality for functions in a bounded two-dimensional domain containing the origin. It states that for any positive alpha and beta between zero and two, a certain weighted exponential integral is finite. The supremum of this integral over functions with norm at most one is bounded by a constant depending on the domain. This supremum is finite if and only if alpha divided by four pi plus beta divided by two is less than or equal to one.
returned_results.name: Lemma 2.4

returned_results.slogan: The theorem establishes an inequality for functions in the Sobolev space H1,2 on a set Sigma. It applies to functions u whose exponential averages over two well-separated subsets Omega1 and Omega2 are each at least some fixed positive fraction of the total exponential average. The inequality bounds the integral of e to the u over Sigma by a constant times an exponential expression involving the squared norm of the gradient of u and the integral of u. The constant depends on the separation distance between the subsets, the lower bounds on the averages, and an arbitrarily small positive parameter epsilon.
returned_results.name: Lemma 3.3

returned_results.slogan: For dimension two, the Moser-Trudinger inequality implies an upper bound on the logarithm of the exponential integral in terms of the squared gradient norm and the function's average, with a constant dependent on beta. For dimension four, an Adams-type inequality gives an upper bound on the same logarithm using the norm of the operator applied to the function, plus a small parameter eta and a constant. Both results hold for functions in appropriate Sobolev spaces over their respective domains.
returned_results.name: Lemma A.3

returned_results.slogan: For two points with equal and opposite weights, if the minimum weight is positive and the function h meets a given condition, then the Moser-Trudinger functional is bounded below on a radial function space. This holds for any parameter value less than eight pi times one plus the minimum weight.
returned_results.name: Lemma 2.1

returned_results.slogan: A Moser-Trudinger inequality on domains implies a monotonicity property for the integral of Green's function. This in turn implies a Nash-Sobolev inequality on the entire surface. Under additional geometric conditions on the area and length of geodesic balls, the Nash-Sobolev inequality also implies the Green's function monotonicity.
returned_results.name: Theorem 5.3

returned_results.slogan: The sharp subcritical Moser-Trudinger inequality follows from the sharp critical version. If a certain constant is finite, then another related constant is also finite. An upper bound is provided for this constant in terms of the critical constant. A specific case gives a simplified bound when parameters take particular values.
returned_results.name: Lemma 2.2

returned_results.slogan: The Trudinger-Moser inequality for unbounded domains states that for any function in the Sobolev space H^1 over the plane, the integral of e raised to alpha times the square of the function's absolute value minus one is finite for every positive alpha. If the L^2 norm of the gradient is at most one and the L^2 norm of the function is bounded by some finite M, and if alpha is less than 4 pi, then this integral is bounded by a constant that depends only on M and alpha. This constant is independent of the specific function, provided these conditions hold. The result extends a classical inequality to functions defined on the entire plane.
returned_results.name: Lemma 3.1

returned_results.slogan: The Moser-Trudinger-Onofri inequality is obtained as the limiting case of the Sobolev inequality.
returned_results.name: Theorem 1

returned_results.slogan: Given disjoint subsets of a surface with a minimum separation distance and each subset containing a significant portion of the exponential of a function, an inequality holds. The left side involves logarithmic integrals of the exponential of the function over the whole surface and its boundary. The right side is bounded by a small multiple of the Dirichlet energy plus a linear term in the function and a constant. The constant depends on the chosen small parameter.
returned_results.name: Lemma 4.6

returned_results.slogan: On a compact Riemannian surface, given a nonzero mean smooth function and two separated subsets with positive distance, an inequality bounds the exponential integral of any function in the Sobolev space. The bound depends on the gradient norm and the average of the function, scaled by a constant that incorporates separation distance and subset mass thresholds. The inequality holds provided the function assigns a minimum fraction of its exponential mass to each of the two subsets. The constant also depends on an arbitrarily small positive parameter.
returned_results.name: Lemma 15

trajectory.query: Hadamard formula first variation of energy domain integral with Robin boundary condition shape derivative torsional rigidity

returned_results.slogan: The derivative of the torsional rigidity with respect to a deformation direction equals the boundary integral of the squared gradient of the torsion function multiplied by the normal component of the deformation field. This holds for open, bounded sets with a continuously differentiable boundary. The torsion function is specific to the domain. The outer unit normal vector is used in the calculation.
returned_results.name: Theorem 2.4

returned_results.slogan: The torsion of a convex domain equals an integral over its boundary involving the support function and the gradient of the solution to a specific equation. This integral is scaled by a constant factor. The derivative of the torsion with respect to a domain perturbation is given by a similar boundary integral using the support function of the perturbing domain. This derivative describes the first-order change in torsion when the domain is slightly expanded.
returned_results.name: Theorem 5

returned_results.slogan: A smooth variation of a hypersurface embedded in a ball induces a change in the torsion energy of the enclosed domain. The first variation of the torsion energy equals an integral over the hypersurface. The integrand involves the square of the normal derivative of the torsion function. It also includes the inner product of the variation vector field with the unit normal.
returned_results.name: Proposition 4.1

returned_results.slogan: The first eigenvalue of the Robin p-Laplacian on a perturbed domain has two equivalent formulas for its derivative at zero. Both expressions are boundary integrals involving the perturbation's normal component. The integrands include terms with the gradient and absolute value of the eigenfunction, the eigenvalue, mean curvature, and a Robin parameter. The two formulas differ in their specific combination of these terms.
returned_results.name: Theorem 1.2

returned_results.slogan: The shape derivative of the torsional rigidity functional exists at zero. It equals the integral over the boundary of the domain. The integrand is the p-th power of the normal derivative of y multiplied by the inner product of the velocity vector and the outward normal. The integration is with respect to the surface measure.
returned_results.name: Proposition

returned_results.slogan: The shape derivative of the energy functional is continuously differentiable near the initial domain. The derivative at the initial domain is expressed as a boundary integral involving the gradient of the solution to a Dirichlet problem. This derivative can also be written as an integral over the torus using polar coordinates. The derivative is a bounded function on the torus.
returned_results.name: Proposition 3.13

returned_results.slogan: The shape derivative of an integral over a domain is expressed as a boundary integral. The derivative depends on a variation function defined on the boundary. The result involves integrating the product of the original function and the variation along the boundary. This formula applies to sufficiently smooth variations.
returned_results.name: Lemma 5.1

returned_results.slogan: The shape derivative of an energy functional for a domain in the plane is given by a boundary integral involving the gradient of the solution and the normal component of a vector field. The second derivative involves additional boundary and domain integrals under higher regularity assumptions. The first and second variations of the transformed solution are characterized by specific partial differential equations. These derivatives describe how the energy changes as the domain is perturbed.
returned_results.name: Proposition 2.6

returned_results.slogan: The Hadamard shape derivative for a simple eigenvalue of a Dirichlet problem is given by an integral over the boundary of the domain. The integrand involves the square of the second normal derivative of the eigenfunction. This expression is multiplied by the normal component of the velocity field. The domain is assumed to be bounded and of class C4.
returned_results.name: Theorem 5.1

returned_results.slogan: For a bounded domain with smooth boundary and zero Dirichlet boundary conditions, the derivative of the energy functional with respect to shape variations is given by an integral over the boundary. This integral involves the squared magnitude of the gradient of the solution to the Laplace equation. The derivative depends on the normal component of the variation field. The result is expressed as a boundary integral with respect to the surface measure.
returned_results.name: Theorem 5.7

trajectory.query: Reynolds transport theorem derivative of integral over moving domain and boundary surface integral

returned_results.slogan: The time derivative of the integral of a function over a moving domain equals the integral of its partial time derivative plus the boundary integral of the function multiplied by the domain's velocity and the outward normal. This applies to smooth functions and smoothly evolving domains. The result is a generalization of the Reynolds transport theorem. It accounts for changes due to both the function's explicit time dependence and the domain's motion.
returned_results.name: Theorem 2.5

returned_results.slogan: The Reynolds transport theorem relates the time derivative of an integral over a moving volume to the integral of the partial time derivative and a surface integral. It applies to a smoothly deforming domain and a differentiable scalar field. The change in the integral equals the integral of the time derivative plus the flux of the field through the boundary. The flux term involves the velocity of the domain's boundary and the outer unit normal.
returned_results.name: Proposition 1.1

returned_results.slogan: The time derivative of the integral of a function over a moving domain equals the integral of the partial time derivative over the domain plus the flux of the function across the boundary. The flux term involves the function multiplied by the normal component of the domain's velocity. This result holds for continuously differentiable functions defined on Euclidean space and non-negative time. It is a version of the Reynolds transport theorem.
returned_results.name: Lemma 3.3

returned_results.slogan: The Reynolds transport theorem relates the time derivative of an integral over a moving volume to the sum of two integrals. The first integral accounts for the local rate of change of the integrand inside the volume. The second integral accounts for the flux of the integrand across the moving boundary. The velocity of the boundary and the outer unit normal are used to compute this flux.
returned_results.name: Proposition 1.2

returned_results.slogan: The time derivative of the integral of a function over a moving domain equals the integral of the partial time derivative of the function plus the divergence of the function multiplied by the velocity field. This holds for a continuously differentiable function defined on a time-dependent region in three-dimensional space. The domain evolves according to a flow generated by a smooth vector field. The result is a version of the Reynolds transport theorem.
returned_results.name: Theorem D.13 (Reynold’s Transport Theorem)

returned_results.slogan: The time derivative of the integral of a function over a moving control volume equals the integral of the partial time derivative of the function plus the divergence of the function multiplied by the velocity field. This holds for a smoothly moving volume and a sufficiently smooth function. The result is a form of the Reynolds transport theorem.
returned_results.name: Theorem 2.1 (see~ \cite{Rey03}, Eq.(16) and \cite{ChoM93}, p.10)

returned_results.slogan: The time derivative of the integral of a function over a moving domain equals the integral of the partial time derivative plus the divergence of the function multiplied by the velocity field. This holds for a continuously differentiable function and a flow generated by a smooth vector field. The domain evolves over time according to the flow map. The result is a generalization of the Reynolds transport theorem.
returned_results.name: Theorem B.4 (Reynold’s Transport Theorem)

returned_results.slogan: The time derivative of the integral of a smooth field over a time-dependent domain equals the integral of the partial time derivative of the field over the domain plus the integral of the field multiplied by the normal velocity over the boundary. The domain can be two or three-dimensional and may have multiple holes. The boundary moves with a given velocity, and the unit normal points outward. This result is a generalization of the Reynolds transport theorem.
returned_results.name: Theorem 1 (Transport theorem for generic time dependent domains)

returned_results.slogan: Reynolds's transport theorem describes the rate of change of an integral over a moving volume. The volume changes shape over time according to a smooth deformation. The derivative equals the integral of the partial time derivative of the function plus a boundary term. The boundary term involves the dot product of the velocity field and the outward unit normal, integrated over the surface.
returned_results.name: Proposition \thechapter .10

returned_results.slogan: The time derivative of a volume integral over a domain moving with Lipschitz velocity equals the integral of the material derivative plus the product of the function and the divergence of the velocity. For a surface integral over a hypersurface moving with divergence-free velocity, the time derivative equals the integral of the material derivative minus a term involving the normal component of the velocity gradient. These formulas extend the Reynolds transport theorem to time-dependent domains and surfaces. They describe how integrals change due to both the function's evolution and the domain's motion.
returned_results.name: Proposition 2.4

trajectory.query: shape derivative of solution to elliptic PDE with Robin boundary condition first variation

returned_results.slogan: Given a sufficiently smooth domain and vector field, a function in a certain Sobolev space is shape differentiable. Its derivative solves a specific boundary value problem. The problem involves Laplace's equation in the domain with zero Dirichlet and Robin-type boundary conditions. The Robin condition on part of the boundary includes terms involving surface divergence, curvature, and the normal component of the vector field.
returned_results.name: Lemma 4.2

returned_results.slogan: The solution u_N in H^1(Omega) is shape differentiable with respect to the domain Omega in the direction V. Its shape derivative u'_N in H^1(Omega) is the unique solution to a boundary value problem. The problem involves Laplace's equation in the interior and Neumann and Robin conditions on the boundary. The Robin condition on Gamma includes a term Upsilon(u_N)[V_n] defined using surface divergence, tangential gradients, mean curvature, and boundary data.
returned_results.name: Lemma 3.6.1 (\cite{AfraitesRabago2022})

returned_results.slogan: The shape derivative of a cost functional under a Robin constraint is expressed as a sum of integrals over the domain and its boundary. The integrands involve specific vector and tensor fields defined in terms of given functions and their derivatives. These fields are constructed from the state variable, an adjoint variable, and other smooth input functions. The result holds under regularity and positivity conditions on the domain and the functions involved.
returned_results.name: Proposition 1

returned_results.slogan: The solution u_D belongs to the H^3 Sobolev space and is shape differentiable with respect to the domain in the direction of the vector field V. Its shape derivative u'_D is in H^1 and uniquely satisfies a Laplace equation in the domain with homogeneous Dirichlet conditions on one boundary. On another boundary, it satisfies a Robin-type condition involving a linear operator applied to u_D and the normal component of V. The operator includes tangential divergence and gradient terms, as well as terms involving the normal derivative, the mean curvature, and a constant.
returned_results.name: Lemma 3.2.1 (\cite{AfraitesRabago2022})

returned_results.slogan: Given elements in certain function spaces have shape derivatives. The solution to a Dirichlet boundary value problem then has a shape derivative in a Sobolev space. This derivative is the unique solution to another boundary value problem. It satisfies a Poisson equation with a given right-hand side and a specific boundary condition involving the normal derivative and another shape derivative term.
returned_results.name: Proposition 4.1

returned_results.slogan: The first eigenvalue of the Robin p-Laplacian on a perturbed domain has two equivalent formulas for its derivative at zero. Both expressions are boundary integrals involving the perturbation's normal component. The integrands include terms with the gradient and absolute value of the eigenfunction, the eigenvalue, mean curvature, and a Robin parameter. The two formulas differ in their specific combination of these terms.
returned_results.name: Theorem 1.2

returned_results.slogan: The shape derivative of an integral over a domain is expressed as a boundary integral. The derivative depends on a variation function defined on the boundary. The result involves integrating the product of the original function and the variation along the boundary. This formula applies to sufficiently smooth variations.
returned_results.name: Lemma 5.1

returned_results.slogan: The shape derivative of a solution to a weak formulation exists under certain regularity conditions. It is defined as the limit of the difference between perturbed and original solutions as the perturbation parameter goes to zero. The derivative satisfies a specific partial differential equation system in the domain. Boundary conditions involve the normal component of the perturbation field and the original solution's gradient.
returned_results.name: Theorem 3.3

returned_results.slogan: The shape derivative of the first eigenfunction satisfies a boundary value problem. It is governed by a Poisson equation with a source term involving the eigenvalue and its derivative. On the Dirichlet boundary, the derivative equals the negative normal derivative of the eigenfunction multiplied by the normal component of the vector field. On the Neumann boundary, the normal derivative of the shape derivative involves terms with the gradient of the eigenfunction and the vector field.
returned_results.name: Lemma A.9

returned_results.slogan: Given a continuously varying boundary condition parameterized by t, the Robin elliptic operator remains self-adjoint. A Krein-type formula relates the resolvent differences of these operators at different parameter values. The resolvent depends differentiably on t and satisfies a Riccati equation. The derivative of an isolated eigenvalue is expressed in terms of the derivative of the boundary parameter and the boundary traces of corresponding eigenfunctions.
returned_results.name: Theorem 8.2

trajectory.query: derivative of surface integral over moving boundary mean curvature term formula

returned_results.slogan: The derivative of the surface integral of a function over a moving boundary equals the integral of a specific combination of partial derivatives. This combination includes the time derivative of the function, the normal derivative scaled by the normal velocity, and the function multiplied by the mean curvature and normal velocity. The boundary is deformed by a smooth velocity field, and the function is continuously differentiable. The result holds for small time values.
returned_results.name: Theorem 2

returned_results.slogan: The time derivative of the integral of a smooth surface field over a moving submanifold equals the integral of the material derivative plus the field times the surface divergence of the velocity. It also equals the integral of the partial time derivative plus terms involving the normal velocity and mean curvature, plus a boundary integral term. The boundary term involves the field and the velocity dotted with the co-normal. The mean curvature and normal velocity components are defined in terms of the surface normal and material velocity.
returned_results.name: Theorem Appendix\unhbox \voidb@x \protect \penalty \@M \ A.{2}

returned_results.slogan: The derivative with respect to time of the integral of a function over a moving surface equals an integral involving the function's time derivative and Laplacian. It also includes a negative term with the squared norm of a vector sum involving the mean curvature and a position vector. An additional positive term involves the function multiplied by the squared norm of the second fundamental form. This identity holds for a smooth family of compactly supported functions on the evolving surface.
returned_results.name: Lemma 2.1 (Huisken’s monotonicity formula)

returned_results.slogan: The time derivative of the integral of a function over a moving surface equals the integral of the function's material derivative plus the function multiplied by the surface divergence of the velocity field. This can also be expressed using the tangential part of the velocity and the mean curvature. For a function defined in the surrounding space, the derivative involves the partial time derivative and the surface divergence of the function times the velocity. It also includes terms with the normal derivative of the function and the normal component of velocity.
returned_results.name: Theorem \thesection .3 (Transport Theorem for Moving Surfaces in $\mathbb {R}^3$)

returned_results.slogan: The surface divergence theorem relates the integral of the surface divergence to the mean curvature and boundary terms. For a vector field on a moving surface, the integral of its surface divergence equals minus the integral of the mean curvature times the normal component, plus the boundary flux. The mean curvature is defined as the negative surface divergence of the unit normal vector. The boundary term involves the unit outer co-normal vector along the surface's edge.
returned_results.name: Lemma 3.8 (Surface divergence theorem)

returned_results.slogan: A compact evolving hypersurface with a velocity field and a function defined on it satisfies a time derivative formula for the surface integral. The derivative equals the integral of the function's normal time derivative plus its product with the surface divergence of the velocity. This can also be expressed using the tangential velocity and the mean curvature, or via a different time derivative and a boundary term. The boundary term involves the function, the velocity, and the outer unit conormal along the boundary.
returned_results.name: Theorem 32

returned_results.slogan: The rate of change of the area of a surface equals the integral of the mean curvature times the normal speed over the surface, plus a boundary term involving the normal and the time derivative of the boundary parametrization.
returned_results.name: Proposition 14

returned_results.slogan: The rate of change of the area of a surface moving in a manifold equals an integral over the surface of the mean curvature times the normal motion, plus a boundary term. The boundary term involves the outward normal to the surface's boundary and the outward normal to the manifold's boundary. This formula accounts for both the interior deformation and the boundary behavior of the surface.
returned_results.name: Lemma 2.2 (The first free variation formula)

returned_results.slogan: The time derivative of the integral of a function over a moving surface equals the integral of the inner product of the function's gradient with the gradient of the signed distance, minus the integral of the function multiplied by the mean curvature. The signed distance is defined as the distance to the surface, positive inside and negative outside. This holds for all times before a certain limit and for continuously differentiable functions. The formula relates the rate of change to geometric and analytic properties of the evolving surface.
returned_results.name: Lemma 3.8

returned_results.slogan: The time derivative of the integral of a function over an evolving surface equals the integral of its partial time derivative plus an additional term. The probability of this event is at least one minus a constant times a power of the ratio of two radii.
returned_results.name: Lemma 3.1

returned_results.slogan: At critical probability, planar Voronoi percolation satisfies the strong RSW condition. The probability of a horizontal crossing in an annulus decays polynomially with size. There exist positive constants C and alpha such that the crossing probability is bounded by C divided by R to the power alpha. This holds for all R greater than or equal to 1.
returned_results.name: Theorem 3.8

returned_results.slogan: For a graph with a proper embedding and bounded masses, consider the FK-Ising model on a square with perturbed coupling constants and free boundary conditions. The probability of an open circuit in the annulus between half the width and the full width is bounded below by a positive constant. This constant depends only on the mass bound and embedding parameters. A comparable bound applies to the dual model.
returned_results.name: Theorem 2.4

trajectory.query: For any positive epsilon limit as eta approaches zero limsup delta probability of E_delta eta epsilon boundary arc is zero outermost Ising loops do not contact boundary

returned_results.slogan: For any positive epsilon, the limit as eta approaches zero of the upper limit as delta goes to zero of the probability of event E sub delta of eta, epsilon, and partial Omega is zero. This implies that in the scaling limit, the outermost Ising loops almost surely do not contact the boundary.
returned_results.name: Lemma 11

returned_results.slogan: For every positive epsilon, there exists a positive eta such that almost surely, the limit inferior as time goes to infinity of the measure of points within distance eta of the boundary is at most epsilon.
returned_results.name: Proposition 4.1

returned_results.slogan: For any positive epsilon, there exists a positive delta zero depending on epsilon and eta such that for any domain in a specified class, if delta and alpha are less than delta zero, then the probability that a certain path hits a particular set given it starts near a boundary point is less than epsilon.
returned_results.name: Lemma 6.3

returned_results.slogan: For sufficiently small epsilon and large N, the supremum over x in the boundary of M_epsilon of the probability that the absolute value of p_epsilon at the stopping time is less than or equal to delta and the stopping time is at most r converges to zero as delta approaches zero.
returned_results.name: Lemma 5.7

returned_results.slogan: For a CLE with parameter between 4 and 8, given any positive epsilon, there is a positive delta depending on epsilon. For any Borel subset of the boundary with Lebesgue measure at least epsilon, the probability is at least delta that the outermost loop surrounding the origin intersects that subset.
returned_results.name: Lemma A.3

returned_results.slogan: As epsilon approaches zero, the conditional distribution of gamma zero given that it avoids the disk of radius epsilon converges to the distribution of the outer boundary of Psi zero of theta zero. This convergence is weak with respect to the Hausdorff topology on compact sets.
returned_results.name: Proposition 4.2 (Proposition 4.1 in \cite {MR2979861})

returned_results.slogan: For any positive delta and eta, almost surely there exists a small positive epsilon zero. For sufficiently large L, any two points x and y far from the boundary by at least delta are connected by a path. This path remains at least epsilon zero away from the boundary. The path length is at most the distance between x and y plus eta.
returned_results.name: Lemma 9

returned_results.slogan: For any positive delta, as epsilon approaches zero, the supremum over u in B sub c of the absolute difference between P sub u of the event that tau sub epsilon of partial G is between e to the power of Delta minus delta over epsilon squared and e to the power of Delta plus delta over epsilon squared and one converges to zero.
returned_results.name: Theorem 4.1

returned_results.slogan: In the critical Ising model with plus boundary conditions on a discretized Jordan domain, the set of all leftmost Ising loops converges in law to the nested CLE3 as the mesh size goes to zero. With high probability, any macroscopic Ising loop is close to a leftmost loop. Specifically, for any positive epsilon, as the mesh size decreases, the probability tends to one that for every large loop there is a leftmost loop such that their symmetric difference consists of connected components with diameter less than epsilon. This establishes a strong geometric resemblance between macroscopic and leftmost loops at criticality.
returned_results.name: Theorem 3

returned_results.slogan: For each fixed s less than t, the limit of epsilon raised to d_gamma times N_epsilon of the epsilon boundary of eta from s to t is almost surely zero as epsilon approaches zero. As a result, the difference between epsilon to d_gamma times N_epsilon and epsilon to d_gamma times N_epsilon superscript circle of eta from s to t also converges to zero almost surely.
returned_results.name: Lemma 4.4

trajectory.query: topological rectangle crossing of minus spins mixed boundary conditions critical Ising positive probability lemma

returned_results.slogan: For any positive length L, there exists a positive constant eta depending on L such that the following holds. Consider any topological rectangle with cross-length at most L. The probability of a crossing of minus one spins between two opposite sides is at least eta. This holds for the critical Ising model with specified mixed boundary conditions.
returned_results.name: Corollary 1.7

returned_results.slogan: For each positive M, there exists a positive eta depending on M. For any discrete topological rectangle with boundary arcs separated by distance at most M, the probability of a crossing between two opposite arcs is at least eta. This holds under mixed boundary conditions: free on the two crossing arcs and fixed negative on the other two arcs. The result applies at the critical inverse temperature.
returned_results.name: Theorem 14

returned_results.slogan: For each positive L, there exists a constant c(L) greater than zero. This holds for any discrete topological rectangle where the distance between two opposite sides is at most L. The probability of a crossing event under mixed boundary conditions is at least c(L). The boundary conditions are free on two opposite sides and fixed to minus on the other two.
returned_results.name: Lemma 3.10

returned_results.slogan: The Ising model with free or plus boundary conditions in a rectangle has dimensions n and m, where m is less than beta times n. There exists a positive constant c sub beta. The probability of a vertical plus crossing occurring is at least c sub beta. This holds for both free and plus boundary conditions.
returned_results.name: Corollary 16

returned_results.slogan: For any positive L, there exists a positive constant c(L) such that for any topological rectangle with distance at most L between two opposite sides, the probability of a plus connection between these sides is at least c(L). The boundary conditions are free on these two sides and minus on the remaining two sides. This holds at the critical inverse temperature. The constant depends only on L and not on the specific rectangle.
returned_results.name: Proposition 5.3 (RSW for topological rectangle)

returned_results.slogan: For all positive k and l at least four-thirds, there exists a constant c depending on k and l such that the probability of a horizontal crossing in a specific rectangle is at least c. The rectangle spans from negative k times n to positive k times n in width and from zero to n in height. The crossing event is considered within a larger domain that extends the height to l times n. The probability is measured under a random-cluster model with mixed boundary conditions: free on the bottom and wired on the other three sides.
returned_results.name: Lemma 3

returned_results.slogan: For the two-dimensional Ising model above the critical probability, the probability of a vertical crossing in a finite rectangle with free boundary conditions is at least one minus an exponentially small term. The bound decays exponentially in the side length to the power of one less than the dimension. This holds for sufficiently large rectangles and a specific width parameter. The constant in the exponent depends on the probability parameter.
returned_results.name: Corollary 3.1

returned_results.slogan: For any positive alpha, consider a rectangular domain and its semi-discretized version with a boundary condition. The probability of a horizontal crossing occurring in this domain is bounded away from zero and one. Similarly, the probability of a vertical crossing is also bounded away from zero and one. These bounds hold uniformly in the size and discretization of the domain.
returned_results.name: Proposition 5.7 (RSW property)

returned_results.slogan: For a fixed positive lambda, there exist positive constants C7 and M such that for all n greater than zero and p exceeding p_c minus lambda over n, two crossing probabilities are bounded below by C7. The first probability is for a horizontal crossing in a rectangle of width 2Mn and height n, with specific boundary conditions. The second probability is for a vertical crossing in a rectangle of width 2Mn and height Mn, also with given boundary conditions. Both probabilities are uniformly bounded away from zero.
returned_results.name: Proposition 2.9

returned_results.slogan: For a critical FK model on a rectangular lattice with specific dimensions, the vertical crossing probability of a centered sub-rectangle is bounded away from zero. This holds for parameters within a given range. The bound depends on the aspect ratio and the margin from the boundary. The result applies to all sufficiently large scales.
returned_results.name: Theorem ({\cite[Theorem 3)

trajectory.query: Hovey correspondence abelian model category from two compatible complete hereditary cotorsion pairs

returned_results.slogan: Under certain conditions on a bicomplete Abelian category with a complete hereditary cotorsion pair, two specific pairs in the chain complex category are complete cotorsion pairs. These pairs are compatible, forming a Hovey triple that gives an Abelian model structure. The homotopy category of this model structure is equivalent to the derived category of the original Abelian category.
returned_results.name: Proposition 8.6

returned_results.slogan: A bicomplete abelian category yields a Hovey triple from a given pair if and only if that pair is a complete hereditary cotorsion pair. The resulting triple is also hereditary. The homotopy category of this triple is equivalent to the derived category of the original abelian category.
returned_results.name: Theorem 5.3 (Models for Derived Categories)

returned_results.slogan: Given a bicomplete Abelian category, if two compatible cotorsion pairs exist with a thick class, then there is a unique Abelian model structure with specified classes of cofibrant, fibrant, and trivial objects. Conversely, any Abelian model structure yields two compatible and complete cotorsion pairs from its cofibrant, fibrant, and trivial object classes.
returned_results.name: Theorem 1.1 (M. Hovey, {\cite[Theorem 2.2]{Hovey}})

returned_results.slogan: Hovey's theorem establishes a bijection between abelian model structures and Hovey triples in a bicomplete abelian category. This correspondence maps each abelian model structure to a triple consisting of cofibrant, trivial, and fibrant objects. The result shows that these two classifications are equivalent. The theorem is attributed to Hovey.
returned_results.name: Theorem 13

returned_results.slogan: The Hovey correspondence establishes a bijection between abelian model structures and Hovey triples in an abelian category. It maps the classes of cofibrant, fibrant, and trivial objects to the corresponding cofibrations, fibrations, and weak equivalences. The inverse assigns to a triple of classes the associated model structure defined via specific conditions on monomorphisms and epimorphisms. This correspondence is explicit and mutually inverse.
returned_results.name: Theorem 2.6

returned_results.slogan: Hovey's Lemma 6.7 states that in a Grothendieck category with enough projectives, two compatible cotorsion pairs each cogenerated by a set yield a cofibrantly generated abelian model structure.
returned_results.name: Proposition 5.2

returned_results.slogan: Given a right trivial extension of an abelian category with certain conditions, a hereditary complete cotorsion pair is constructed. The pair involves specified classes and has a contravariantly finite intersection. An equivalence of homotopy categories is established between model categories associated with these intersections.
returned_results.name: Theorem 3.20

returned_results.slogan: The class of contravariantly finite hereditary complete cotorsion pairs in an abelian category corresponds bijectively to the class of weakly projective model structures. Each cotorsion pair maps to a model structure defined by its core. The associated homotopy category is equivalent to the additive quotient of the first component by the core.
returned_results.name: Theorem 2.11

returned_results.slogan: Given two complete hereditary cotorsion pairs in an abelian category with certain containments and equalities, there exists a unique cofibrantly generated abelian model structure. The trivial objects in this model structure are those that fit into a short exact sequence with objects from the specified classes. Specifically, an object is trivial if it is the kernel of a surjection from an object in one class to an object in another, or if it is the cokernel of an injection from one class to another. The two characterizations of trivial objects are equivalent.
returned_results.name: Lemma 4.2

returned_results.slogan: In a bicomplete Abelian category with a cotorsion pair and exact complexes, under completeness conditions and an equality of classes, the triple of exact complexes and two dg-classes forms a Hovey triple. This induces an Abelian model structure on the category of chain complexes. The weak equivalences are quasi-isomorphisms. Cofibrations are monomorphisms with cokernel in the first dg-class, and fibrations are epimorphisms with kernel in the second dg-class.
returned_results.name: Corollary 1.7

trajectory.query: F-totally acyclic complexes flat quasi-coherent sheaves model structure Corollary 3.12 BEGI

returned_results.slogan: An injective exact model structure exists on the category of complexes of quasi-coherent flat sheaves over a scheme. Every object is cofibrant, and fibrant objects are dg-cotorsion complexes that are flat in each degree. The trivial objects are acyclic complexes with flat cycles. The homotopy category is the derived category of flat sheaves.
returned_results.name: Theorem 5.4

returned_results.slogan: Given certain conditions on the sheaf A and its quasi-coherent sections, an abelian model category structure exists on the chain complex category of quasi-coherent sheaves. This structure is defined by a specific triple involving F-tac of A quasi-coherent, a class W, and dg of B. The homotopy category of this model structure is triangulated equivalent to the category induced by F-tac of flat sheaves. This equivalence arises from a Quillen equivalence between the corresponding model categories.
returned_results.name: Theorem 7.3

returned_results.slogan: An acyclic complex of flat cotorsion sheaves on a semi-separated noetherian space is totally acyclic exactly when it is F-totally acyclic.
returned_results.name: Proposition 4.2

returned_results.slogan: The pair consisting of the bounded acyclic complex of flat sheaves and the bounded complex of cotorsion sheaves forms a complete cotorsion theory in the bounded derived category of quasi-coherent sheaves.
returned_results.name: Theorem 2.4

returned_results.slogan: A ring where all level modules have finite projective dimension implies that a complex of projectives is cofibrant in the firmly acyclic model structure exactly when it is totally acyclic. If the ring is right coherent, the condition can be relaxed to all flat modules having finite projective dimension.
returned_results.name: Corollary 6.9

returned_results.slogan: An F-totally acyclic complex of flat quasi-coherent sheaves on a scheme is defined by the existence of an affine open covering. For each open set in this covering, the complex of flat modules over the ring of sections must be F-totally acyclic. This condition ensures the property holds locally on the scheme.
returned_results.name: Corollary 2.8

returned_results.slogan: A bounded below complex of cotorsion flat sheaves, as an object in the homotopy category of flat sheaves, lies in the orthogonal complement of the category of totally acyclic complexes of flat sheaves.
returned_results.name: Lemma 4.13

returned_results.slogan: For a semi-separated coherent scheme, there is an exact AC-acyclic flat model structure on chain complexes of quasi-coherent sheaves. The cofibrant objects are exact AC-acyclic complexes of flat sheaves with Gorenstein flat cycles. Trivially cofibrant objects are exact complexes of flat sheaves with categorically flat cycles. In the affine case, the homotopy category corresponds to that of Ding projective modules.
returned_results.name: Theorem 1.2

returned_results.slogan: The composite of canonical functors from the homotopy category of F-totally acyclic complexes of flat cotorsion modules to the quotient of the homotopy category of F-totally acyclic complexes of flat modules by the homotopy category of pure acyclic complexes of flat modules is a triangulated equivalence.
returned_results.name: Theorem 5.6

returned_results.slogan: A complex of flat sheaves is N-totally acyclic if and only if it is acyclic and the Hom complex into every cotorsion flat sheaf is also acyclic. Equivalently, it is both left and right orthogonal in the homotopy category to all shifts of flat sheaves. Another equivalent condition is that the complex is acyclic and the mapping complex into every flat sheaf is acyclic. These four statements characterize the same property for such complexes.
returned_results.name: Theorem 4.18

trajectory.query: localization of cotorsion pairs to quasi-coherent sheaves over scheme generated by a set hereditary cotorsion pair

returned_results.slogan: Flat quasi-coherent sheaves and cotorsion quasi-coherent sheaves form a hereditary complete cotorsion pair in the category of quasi-coherent sheaves on a quasi-compact semi-separated scheme. This pair satisfies the necessary conditions for a cotorsion theory. The result holds in the abelian category structure of quasi-coherent sheaves. The theorem applies specifically to schemes with these topological and separation properties.
returned_results.name: Theorem 8.1

returned_results.slogan: A quasi-compact semi-separated scheme has a hereditary complete cotorsion pair in its contraherent cosheaf category. This pair consists of antilocally flat contraherent cosheaves and locally cotorsion contraherent cosheaves. The cotorsion pair holds in the exact category of contraherent cosheaves over the scheme.
returned_results.name: Theorem 8.7

returned_results.slogan: A quasi-compact semi-separated scheme has a hereditary complete cotorsion pair in its contraherent cosheaf category. This pair consists of antilocal contraherent cosheaves and locally injective contraherent cosheaves. The cotorsion pair holds in the exact category of contraherent cosheaves.
returned_results.name: Theorem 8.6

returned_results.slogan: Quasi-compact semi-separated schemes have a hereditary complete cotorsion pair in their quasi-coherent sheaf category. This pair consists of very flat quasi-coherent sheaves and contraadjusted quasi-coherent sheaves. The pair satisfies the necessary conditions for a cotorsion theory. It is both complete and hereditary.
returned_results.name: Theorem 8.2

returned_results.slogan: Given a commutative ring R and a multiplicative subset S, consider a hereditary cotorsion pair cogenerated by a set of pure-injectives. There exists a corresponding hereditary cotorsion pair in the module category over the localization R_S, also cogenerated by a set of pure-injectives. The class of this new pair is the intersection of the original class with the localized module category. Furthermore, the i-th component of the localized cotorsion pair matches the localization of the i-th component of the original pair for all non-negative integers i.
returned_results.name: Lemma 3.3

returned_results.slogan: A noetherian scheme with enough locally free sheaves has a complete cotorsion pair formed by two classes of sheaves. The first class consists of sheaves orthogonal to the perpendicular of all locally free generators. The second class is the perpendicular of these generators. Every sheaf in the first class is locally projective and quasi-coherent.
returned_results.name: Theorem

returned_results.slogan: Given a ring-valued functor R such that the category of quasi-coherent sheaves over R is equivalent to that of a quasi-projective scheme X over an affine scheme, the category of quasi-coherent sheaves over R has a locally projective generator. This implies the existence of a functorially complete hereditary cotorsion pair. The pair consists of the class of vector bundles over R and its orthogonal complement.
returned_results.name: Proposition 8.18

returned_results.slogan: Given a scheme X and a class of modules A contained in the flat modules, if A is Zariski-local, forms a hereditary cotorsion pair generated by a set on affine opens, has trivial flat A-periodic modules, and satisfies a pushforward condition, then there is an abelian model category structure on chain complexes of quasi-coherent sheaves. The homotopy category of this model structure is triangulated equivalent to the derived category of flat sheaves. For affine schemes, this homotopy category is triangulated equivalent to the homotopy category of projective modules.
returned_results.name: Theorem 6.1

returned_results.slogan: Let X be any scheme with associated quiver Q_X. Suppose C and L are subclasses of quasi-coherent sheaves on X, and C contains a generator of this category. Then the pair consisting of C and the orthogonal complement of L forms a complete cotorsion pair.
returned_results.name: Corollary 3.11

returned_results.slogan: The class of quasi-coherent sheaves with torsion images on affine open subsets forms a torsion class. This torsion class is part of a hereditary torsion theory. The theory applies to the category of quasi-coherent sheaves over a scheme.
returned_results.name: Proposition 3.1

trajectory.query: Quillen equivalence between model structures induced by two cotorsion pairs same weak equivalences identity functor abelian model categories

returned_results.slogan: In an abelian category with two model structures sharing the same trivial objects, if the cofibrations of the first are contained in those of the second, then the identity functor is a left Quillen equivalence between them. Alternatively, if the fibrations of the second are contained in those of the first, then the identity functor is a right Quillen equivalence in the opposite direction. This establishes conditions under which the identity functor becomes a Quillen equivalence.
returned_results.name: Lemma 5.4

returned_results.slogan: The weak equivalences are the same in both model category structures. This identity functor forms a Quillen equivalence between the two structures.
returned_results.name: Theorem \thesubsection .4

returned_results.slogan: Given a string of adjoint functors and a model category, if both the left-induced and right-induced model structures exist on the target category, then the identity functors form a Quillen equivalence between these two model structures.
returned_results.name: Proposition 1.16

returned_results.slogan: The model structures from two propositions are Quillen equivalent. The identity functor between two categories of modules is left Quillen.
returned_results.name: Lemma 4.4

returned_results.slogan: The pair of functors forms a Quillen equivalence between the given model categories. This means the derived functors induce an equivalence of homotopy categories. The result ensures that the two model structures present the same homotopy theory.
returned_results.name: Theorem \ref{theo:PsTopsSetQuillenEq}

returned_results.slogan: The identity functor forms a Quillen equivalence between the projective and injective model structures on the category of chain complexes over a commutative ring. Projective cofibrations are objectwise cofibrations, and weak equivalences are the same in both structures. This equivalence holds because the identity functor preserves cofibrations and weak equivalences appropriately.
returned_results.name: Proposition 1.20

returned_results.slogan: Any two distinct model structures on a category with the same weak equivalences satisfying certain conditions are equivalent. This equivalence is established through a zigzag of Quillen functors. Each functor in this zigzag is the identity functor on the underlying category.
returned_results.name: Corollary 3.5

returned_results.slogan: The functors form a pair of Quillen equivalences between the model categories of chain complexes. This means they induce an equivalence of homotopy categories. The adjunction preserves weak equivalences and fibrant or cofibrant objects. The result establishes that the two homotopy categories are equivalent.
returned_results.name: Theorem 1.2

returned_results.slogan: The identity functor forms an adjoint pair. This pair induces a Quillen equivalence between two model categories. The first category is that of fibrant objects under certain conditions. The second category is that of cofibrant objects under related conditions.
returned_results.name: Proposition 4.2

returned_results.slogan: The adjoint pair between two model categories forms a Quillen equivalence. This equivalence relates the homotopy theories of these categories. It ensures that derived functors induce an equivalence of homotopy categories. The result holds for the specified categories and functors.
returned_results.name: Theorem

trajectory.query: F-totally acyclic complexes in A versus flat complexes affine case theorem ring hereditary cotorsion pair generated by a set

returned_results.slogan: For a ring R and a right R-module A, the class of A-acyclic complexes of flat modules forms a complete hereditary cotorsion pair cogenerated by a set. This pair consists of the class and its orthogonal complement. Every chain complex admits a surjective cover from this class.
returned_results.name: Theorem 3.7

returned_results.slogan: An acyclic complex of flat cotorsion sheaves on a semi-separated noetherian space is totally acyclic exactly when it is F-totally acyclic.
returned_results.name: Proposition 4.2

returned_results.slogan: The class of all AC-acyclic complexes of flat modules forms a complete hereditary cotorsion pair that is cogenerated by a set. Every chain complex has a surjective cover from this class. These results also apply to the class of exact AC-acyclic complexes of flat modules.
returned_results.name: Corollary 3.11

returned_results.slogan: For any associative ring R, the class of homotopy flat complexes of flat R-modules and the class of acyclic complexes of cotorsion R-modules form a hereditary complete cotorsion pair. This pair exists in the abelian category of complexes of left R-modules. The left class consists of homotopy flat complexes built from flat modules. The right class consists of acyclic complexes built from cotorsion modules.
returned_results.name: Proposition 7.13

returned_results.slogan: The pair consisting of the flat and cotorsion modules over a ring R is a perfect and hereditary cotorsion pair. It is cogenerated by a set. This pair has strong homological properties.
returned_results.name: Lemma 3.3

returned_results.slogan: Given a scheme X with structure sheaf R and an R(U)-module A_U for each open affine U, the class of A_X-acyclic complexes of flat sheaves is a covering class. If the category of quasi-coherent sheaves on X has a flat generator, such as when X is quasi-compact and semi-separated, then every such cover is an epimorphism. This class and its perpendicular form a complete hereditary cotorsion pair cogenerated by a set.
returned_results.name: Theorem 6.5

returned_results.slogan: For a right coherent ring A, an A-complex T satisfies three equivalent conditions. T is a totally acyclic complex of flat-cotorsion modules. Alternatively, T is a complex of flat-cotorsion modules and normal F-totally acyclic. Finally, T is right Flat A-totally acyclic.
returned_results.name: Theorem 4.4

returned_results.slogan: Given a ring homomorphism from R to A where A is projective as a left R-module, the pair of classes consisting of flat A-modules relative to R-projectives and A-modules that are cotorsion relative to A over R forms a hereditary complete cotorsion pair. This pair is generated by a set of objects in the category of A-modules.
returned_results.name: Proposition 11.1

returned_results.slogan: A flat representation R from I to commutative rings yields a complete hereditary cotorsion pair in the category of quasi-coherent sheaves over R if and only if that category has a flat generator. The cotorsion pair consists of the classes of flat and cotorsion sheaves. This equivalence holds functorially.
returned_results.name: Corollary 8.15

returned_results.slogan: The pair formed by the left orthogonal of the intersection of cotorsion and exact modules with that intersection is a complete and hereditary cotorsion pair in the module category. This cotorsion pair is generated by a set. The intersection of the left orthogonal class with the exact modules equals the class of flat modules.
returned_results.name: Lemma 2.4

trajectory.query: period polynomial characterization W_w^+ one equation P(X,Y)-P(Y-X,Y)+P(Y-X,X)=0 even polynomial

returned_results.slogan: For a nonnegative even integer w and k equal to w plus 2, a sum over even indices r between 0 and w of terms involving a_r and products of sigma functions vanishes on a certain space if and only if there exists a modular form of weight k for a specific congruence subgroup. This modular form has a particular even part of its period polynomial given by a sum over the same indices with coefficients a_{w-r} and monomials in X and Y. The result establishes an equivalence between the vanishing condition and the existence of such a modular form.
returned_results.name: Theorem 17 (Tasaka, personal communication)

returned_results.slogan: For an even positive integer k, every polynomial P in the space W sub k minus 2 can be uniquely expressed as the sum of period functions of two cusp forms f and g in S sub k, plus a constant multiple of the polynomial z to the k minus 2 minus 1.
returned_results.name: Theorem 3.1

returned_results.slogan: For even w at least 2, several implications hold concerning sums over nonnegative integers a and b with a plus b equal to w. If the polynomial in X and Y belongs to certain spaces of period polynomials, then weighted sums involving the values J at specified indices vanish modulo the single zeta value of k. The spaces referenced are defined using conditions related to modular forms of weight w plus 2 on a particular level 2 congruence subgroup. The coefficients q sub a b are derived from a transformation of the polynomial P.
returned_results.name: Theorem 4.1

returned_results.slogan: For an odd positive integer w, consider polynomials p and q with specific symmetry properties. If a linear combination of Y times p and the X-derivative of q equals zero, then both p and q must be identically zero. This holds under the given conditions on the weights and symmetry classes of the polynomials.
returned_results.name: Lemma 41

returned_results.slogan: For a nonnegative even integer w, a polynomial p in V_w with a given sign satisfies that a specific linear combination of p and its transformed versions lies in the space V_w with the opposite sign. This property holds precisely when p belongs to the subspace W_w with the same sign.
returned_results.name: Lemma 36

returned_results.slogan: A function w that solves a certain differential equation and is even in the y direction is bounded by a power of the distance from the origin. Under these conditions, w must be a polynomial.
returned_results.name: Theorem A.5 (Liouville Theorem)

returned_results.slogan: Given an odd integer w and a function C in V_w with a given parity, the difference of C evaluated at certain points lies in the dual parity space V_w with opposite sign. This occurs exactly when C can be expressed as X times a polynomial p from a space of weight w-1 with opposite parity, plus the partial derivative with respect to Y of a polynomial q from a space of weight w+1 with the original parity. The polynomials p and q are taken from specific weighted spaces with complementary parity conditions. The equivalence holds without further constraints on the structure of C.
returned_results.name: Lemma 46

returned_results.slogan: For odd n, every P-invariant polynomial on the space is also Weyl invariant. For even n, every even P-invariant polynomial on the space is Weyl invariant. The result depends on the parity of n.

returned_results.slogan: For an odd positive integer w equal to k plus 2, take two cusp forms f and g of weights k minus 1 and k plus 1 for SL2 of the integers. Another equivalent condition is that the socle of the quotient ring times the quotient of the maximal ideal by the product of the ideal and maximal ideal is nonzero. The ideal is also Burch if the depth of the quotient ring is zero and the type of the quotient by the product of the maximal ideal and ideal does not equal the type of the quotient ring plus the minimal number of generators of the ideal. Finally, the ideal is Burch if and only if its extension to the completion of the ring is a Burch ideal.
